articles.title: Vote Yes on Proposition 4: Democracy Shouldn’t Depend on Wealth
articles.author: Sharon Kyle
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A person should not need wealthy friends to run for public office. And a voter’s influence should not depend on the size of a campaign contribution. Those principles sound basic. Yet when raising money becomes the first test of political viability, people with deep pockets gain an advantage before voters ever hear the candidates debate. Community knowledge, public service, and good ideas can take a back seat to access to donors. California’s Proposition 4, the California Fair Elections Act, offers a practical step toward changing that imbalance. On November 3, vote yes. Give communities the power to act Proposition 4 would remove California’s prohibition on public campaign financing for most state and local offices. It would allow governments to establish programs that give qualifying candidates public support for their campaigns. It would not automatically create or fund those programs. That would require subsequent decisions. California Secretary of State That distinction matters. Voters are deciding whether communities should have this tool available at all. Some California cities already do. Los Angeles, San Francisco, Long Beach, Oakland, and Berkeley operate public campaign financing programs under an exception for charter cities. Proposition 4 would open the door more broadly. Why should a community willing to build a fairer campaign system be barred from trying? Make ordinary supporters matter more Consider a nurse, teacher, tenant organizer, or small-business owner with strong community support but few connections to major donors. Running a credible campaign requires reaching voters, and reaching voters costs money. A well-designed public financing program can help bridge that gap. One option is to match small donations with public funds, increasing the value of contributions from ordinary supporters. The Yes on 4 campaign identifies small-donor matching as one model communities could adopt. Proposition 4 itself does not require that particular approach. The democratic promise is straightforward: candidates could have a stronger reason to build broad community support and a better opportunity to compete without relying so heavily on wealthy benefactors. No financing system guarantees good leadership. But fundraising connections should not determine who gets a serious chance to offer it. For progressives, this reaches beyond campaign procedure. The ability to compete for office shapes who can influence housing, wages, healthcare, environmental protection, and public investment. If we want government to respond to people whose needs are routinely overlooked, we should care about the barriers between those people and elected office. Safeguards—and work still to do Proposition 4 includes restrictions. Funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety could not finance campaigns. Candidates receiving public funds would have to meet eligibility requirements and accept spending limits. The money could not cover legal defense costs, fines, or repayment of candidates’ personal campaign loans. Opponents object to spending taxpayer money on campaigns and argue that too many details are left to future policymakers. Those concerns deserve a direct answer: public financing must have clear budgets, transparent reporting, enforceable rules, and meaningful oversight. The Legislative Analyst says future programs could carry significant costs, depending on their design. The measure itself would also produce a few hundred thousand dollars in annual state costs for guidance. Supporting Proposition 4 means accepting responsibility for scrutinizing what comes next. It also means being honest about its limits. The measure does not eliminate private campaign money or guarantee that wealthy interests will lose influence. It permits communities to build an alternative to candidates’ dependence on that money. The League of Women Voters of California, California Nurses Association, California Common Cause, and Consumer Watchdog are among the organizations backing that opportunity. Open the door Frustration with big money in politics is justified. Resignation gives that money a permanent advantage. Proposition 4 offers a concrete action: let California communities create public financing systems that can help qualified candidates compete and give ordinary supporters greater weight. If you have not voted, vote yes on Proposition 4 . If you have, tell friends why it matters. We should judge candidates by their ideas, integrity, and service to their communities. California should give more of them a fair chance to be heard.

articles.title: Book Review: A Model for U.S.-Mexico Cross-Border Solidarity
articles.author: Dan DiMaggio
articles.content: Labor law reform in Mexico has opened up a major opportunity for workers fighting for genuine, independent unions. What can U.S. unions do to support our brothers and sisters there? And how can we build cross-border campaigns to confront our common employers? Unions asking these questions will find valuable ideas in the e-book International Solidarity in Action: The Relationship Between the United Electrical Workers (UE) and Frente Auténtico del Trabajo (FAT) , available for free download here . Author Robin Alexander, retired director of international affairs for UE, led her union’s partnership with the FAT, which began in 1992, during the campaign to oppose the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA). UE members were seeing their employers cut manufacturing jobs in the U.S. and shift production to Mexico. “The UE leadership became convinced that the union needed to find a labor organization it could work with in Mexico,” Alexander writes, “and also that it was essential to connect international work more directly with UE members and with organizing.” In a meeting in Mexico to discuss the campaign against NAFTA, the UE found the FAT—the only Mexican labor organization to oppose NAFTA. Here was a union that had a lot in common with the left-led UE: fiercely independent, with radical roots and leadership. The FAT had long stood out against Mexico's state-dominated unions and fought for workers’ right to form genuine, independent unions. Both unions were concerned about the growing number of jobs that corporations had moved to assembly plants near Mexico’s northern border with the United States, where unions were either nonexistent or a tool of the government’s development strategy of low wages and long hours. “The UE,” Alexander writes, “was interested in seeing the plants organized by a union that would serve as a partner and ally in Mexico and believed that it could provide solidarity, including some leverage, where it continued to represent workers employed by those companies in the U.S… The FAT was eager to organize the plants that were moving across the border, but lacked the resources to do so.” LIKE-MINDED UNIONS Thus kicked off a partnership that has now lasted 30 years. The book contains several case studies of how the UE and the FAT worked together to back each other’s campaigns against employers such as General Electric and Echlin (a transnational auto parts maker later bought by Dana). For U.S. unionists unfamiliar with the obstacles that Mexican workers are facing as they struggle to oust protection unions and replace them with genuine unions, these sections will be particularly valuable. At Echlin, for example, workers attempting to confront dangerous exposure to asbestos and solvents and form a democratic union were met with a barrage of tactics often deployed by employers, official unions, and Mexican labor boards. For instance, workers were refused a copy of their own collective bargaining agreement. The company fired dozens of independent union supporters, and stalled the union election by claiming the independent metal workers union did not have the proper paperwork to represent auto parts workers. Worse, it allowed the official union to deploy 170 thugs, “some wielding metal rods, clubs, and guns,” into the plant on the eve of the election. And workers were forced to vote out loud in front of the company, official union, and labor board officials. TWO-WAY SOLIDARITY The UE supported the FAT’s organizing by filing complaints under NAFTA’s labor side agreement (NAALC), as well as by providing funds, pressuring shareholders, and organizing speaking tours to draw attention to workers’ rights in Mexico. The relationship went both ways, with the FAT providing important material support to UE’s organizing efforts and fight for labor law reforms in the United States. During a UE organizing drive at a Milwaukee foundry, the FAT provided a Mexican organizer—an activist who had been fired from a GE plant in Ciudad Juarez—to help campaign among a predominantly Mexican immigrant workforce. The organizer spread the word that the UE was not like the official unions in Mexico which so many had had bad experiences with. The FAT has also helped draw attention to the severe limitations on labor rights in states like North Carolina—home of UE Local 150, the North Carolina Public Service Workers Union—where many public sector workers are banned from collective bargaining. Mexican unions filed complaints at the International Labor Organization challenging the ban, and the ILO issued a decision that called on North Carolina to repeal it. The FAT also filed a charge under NAALC, and the Mexican government issued a favorable report in response. While North Carolina’s ban still persists, this work has helped legitimize the union and chip away at the law’s aura of invincibility. Alexander writes, “This was tremendously energizing for the low-wage, primarily African-American workers in North Carolina’s public sector because it turned the long-held belief that public sector workers ‘just don’t have that right’ on its head: from the perspective of international human rights law, it is the state’s ban on collective bargaining that is ‘illegal,’ not workers’ attempts to assert their rights.” WORKER TO WORKER Part 3 of the book details worker-to-worker exchanges, which the UE and the FAT used to deepen the solidarity and “undercut the stereotypes that existed” among members on both sides of the border. The UE-FAT exchanges happened in both the U.S. and Mexico, with an emphasis on rank-and-file participation. Members of both unions “toured plants, exchanged experiences, walked picket lines, attended meetings, assisted with organizing drives, taught high school and university classes, and participated in radio and television programs in an effort to share information, learn about each other, and take the information back to their locals and communities.” UE Local 150 members were part of one set of exchanges where they met public sector unionists from Mexico and Quebec (the exchanges were not always just binational). The experience raised their confidence and expectations, and led to the campaign on international law. There have also been exchanges between co-op members of both unions, organizing institutes, and cultural exchanges, including a cross-border mural project. It showed that “the most effective way to educate workers in the United States and in Mexico—and to motivate them to educate others—was through direct contact with each other,” writes Alexander. “I still have a vivid recollection of workers bonding over their mutual outrage that instead of bonuses the company rewarded both groups by buying them pizza.” Although social media and Zoom have made it easier to meet with people around the world, they’re no substitute for the extended, face-to-face interactions that such exchanges allow. Yet there are remarkably few such programs in place—and our labor movements are worse off because of it. Setting up more such programs should be an urgent task—and Alexander’s book provides practical advice to help. EXPANDING OUR VISION There’s also a glaring need for more education for U.S. unionists about what is happening in the labor movement south of the border (not to mention all over the world)—now more important than ever, as our billionaire-backed president whips up hostility against immigrants and workers abroad. One part of UE’s solidarity work was “Mexican Labor News and Analysis,” a monthly summary that lasted from 1996 to 2016. Reviving such a project would be a real contribution to promoting an international perspective among U.S. union members. Although the UE and the FAT are both small, they have played significant roles in expanding the vision of their countries’ labor movements. In Mexico, where, as Alexander writes, “the FAT and their lawyers... were dismissed as dreamers who were a little crazy when they spoke of the need for secret-ballot elections, the elimination of protection contracts, independent labor judges, or registries of unions and contracts,” the 2019 labor law reform included all of those elements. In the U.S., the UE played a significant role in helping a then-obscure socialist candidate named Bernie Sanders win his first election to Congress in 1990, which decades later helped pave the way for Sanders to popularize an unapologetically pro-worker politics in his two presidential campaigns. Similarly, these two unions have set out a path for international solidarity. Could more unions follow their example, and lay the foundation for a growing sense of shared struggle by U.S. and Mexican workers as a counter to the rising forces of right-wing nationalism? Alexander’s book is a great guide for anyone looking to push their unions along that path. A longer version of this article first appeared in New Labor Forum .

articles.title: Genocide Charges Against Israeli Leaders
articles.author: Marjorie Cohn
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A s Israelis went to the polls last Tuesday to decide who will next preside over Israel’s continuing genocide, a U.N. Commission issued a devastating report on the day before the election. It documents how Israel is importing its Gaza strategy of total destruction into the West Bank. And as the Trump administration escalates its efforts to disable the International Criminal Court with punishing sanctions to prevent prosecution of Israeli leaders for their crimes, the Commission’s report recommends that the ICC seriously consider charging Israeli leaders with genocide in addition to war crimes and crimes against humanity. In November 2024, the ICC issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes and crimes against humanity stemming from their actions in Gaza since October 7, 2023. This was the first time the ICC issued arrest warrants against any Israeli official for crimes against the Palestinian people. Netanyahu and Gallant stand charged with the war crimes of starvation as a form of warfare, and intentional attacks on civilians; as well as the crimes against humanity of murder, persecution, and other inhumane acts. Despite the ruling 10 months earlier by the International Court of Justice on Jan. 26, 2024 that Israel was plausibly committing genocide, former ICC Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan did not seek arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant for the crime of genocide. Related: Trump's Attack on the ICC Exposes America's Double Standard on War Crimes Raji Sourani, director of Palestinian Centre for Human Rights, who praised Khan’s May 2024 applications for the arrest warrants, urged the ICC prosecutor to also secure “warrants for the crime of genocide given the staggering evidence of genocidal acts and intent made by top Israeli officials.” Likewise, international law expert Richard Falk, while calling Khan’s requests for warrants against Netanyahu and Gallant “historic,” said the crime of genocide was “the elephant in the room.” He wrote, “Over time I suspect that the failure to address ‘genocide’ will be regarded as the most shocking weakness in the prosecutor’s formal statement.” Now a U.N. Commission is seeking to rectify that weakness. Commission Finds Israel Continues to Commit Genocide Former U.S. Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin, left, with Netanyahu and Gallant in Tel Aviv, Oct. 13, 2023. (DoD, Chad J. McNeeley, CC BY 2.0) The U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel (“the Commission”) transmitted its new report to the General Assembly on Oct. 26. It documented Israeli war crimes, and the crimes against humanity of extermination, persecution, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence as part of a larger attack aimed at subjugating and displacing the Palestinian people. “The intentional killing and injuring of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank combined with Israel’s persistent denial of responsibility form part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians and impose conditions of life that are unliveable,” Srinivasan Muralidhar, chair of the Commission, said in a statement. “Meanwhile, Israel’s expansion of territorial control in Gaza continues to result in the killing and harming of Palestinian civilians who approach or cross the Yellow Line,” he said. The Commission concluded that “Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.” Genocide is defined by the 1948 Genocide Convention as acts committed “with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group,” including killing members of the group, inflicting serious bodily or mental harm on members of the group, or deliberately inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about the group’s physical destruction in whole or in part. Related: The 2026 Midterms May Not End on Election Day 1,400+ Civilians Killed in ‘Ceasefire’ The Commission referenced its earlier 2025 report, which documented Israel’s genocidal act including “deliberately carry[ing] out acts inflicting death and severe bodily and mental harm on Palestinian children,” and “systematically destroying Palestinian life.” It cited the “specific intent of the Israeli authorities to commit genocide against the Palestinian group in Gaza.” Since Oct. 7, 2023, Israeli forces have killed more than 75,000 Palestinians across the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including at least 21,500 children, and 11,000 women. A “so-called ceasefire” (in the Commission’s words) was declared on Oct. 10, 2025. But since then, Israeli forces have killed over 1,431 people, including at least 300 children, and wounded 5,026, as of September 30, 2026. Between January 2025 and August 2026, Israeli military actions drove more than 34,000 Palestinians from their homes. The Commission called it the largest displacement of Palestinians in the West Bank since 1967, when Israel captured the territory from Jordan. In its new report, the Commission noted a “strategic shift” in Israeli military operations in the West Bank since January 2025, including “widespread destruction of Palestinian housing and infrastructure.” Operation Iron Wall “reflects the import of the Gaza strategy of total destruction into West Bank operations.” IDF soldiers raiding Jenin, Occupied West Bank, January 2025, (IDF Spokesperson’s Unit/Wikimedia Commons/ CC BY-SA 3.0) The Commission documented several instances of sexual violence against Palestinians by Israeli authorities in Gaza. They included multiple insertions of a metal detector into the anus of one victim; tying a plastic cord around the genitals of another victim during interrogation for a long period of time; and the rape of a victim with a stick, then forcing him to insert it into his mouth until he vomited. Israel’s acts of sexual violence, the Commission wrote, “continue to be a part of the pattern to destroy the Palestinians as a group in Gaza.” The Commission also documented examples of sexual violence in the West Bank. One victim was gang raped several times with objects while prison guards mocked and photographed him, squeezed his penis, and threatened they would cut it off until he screamed in pain. And the report noted two cases of sexual violence, including rape, against participants in the 2025 Global Sumud Flotilla. The Commission’s Recommendations The Commission recommended that the ICC prosecutor “examine, within its continuing investigation in the Situation in the State of Palestine, the crimes committed in Gaza and the West Bank, including genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes for amendment to existing arrest warrants and addition to future application for arrest warrants.” In addition, the Commission recommended that Israel immediately end the commission of genocide in Gaza, and fulfill its obligations to prevent and punish genocide and incitement to genocide under the Genocide Convention. It also recommended that Israel comply with the July 2024 advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice, immediately end its unlawful occupation of Palestinian territory, stop all new settlement activities, remove all settlers and settlements, and remove all obstacles to the full exercise of the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination. The Commission recommended that Israel fully comply with international human rights law and international humanitarian law in military and law enforcement operations, and stop targeting civilians and civilian objects indispensable to the survival of a people. And it recommended that Israel prosecute and punish all who commit violations of international humanitarian and human rights law. In a statement, the Council on American-Islamic Relations said : “Once again, the United Nations has concluded what has been obvious to all those who have observed Israel’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank. Slaughtering tens of thousands of people, starving an entire civilian population, detaining them in facilities in which they are tortured, expelling tens of thousands more from their homes – these are crimes against humanity and genocide. The murderous Israeli government must be held accountable for its atrocities.” Consortiuum News

articles.title: MAGA Offensive in Latin America
articles.author: John Perry, Roger D. Harris
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Ecuadorian leftist leader Luisa González recently warned that there is “a whole sinister network involving Marco Rubio, MAGA, and Latin American presidents who are destroying our countries to turn Latin America into their backyard.” A few days after her eerily prescient statement, she was arrested on politically motivated charges. MAGA, in this context, refers to the larger US imperial project under Donald Trump. A key tool in MAGA’s offensive in Latin America is the intensified use of “lawfare.” This politically selective use of a country’s legal and judicial institutions against progressives often involves accusations of corruption and related crimes. The term gained prominence during the partisan prosecution of Brazil's Lula da Silva in 2018. Lawfare has since intensified with the rise of MAGA-aligned governments and Washington's escalating intervention across much of the hemisphere, continuing a long history of US interference in the region. The González case in Ecuador Luisa González was the runner-up in the last two Ecuadorian presidential elections, themselves widely believed to have been stolen. On September 12, Ecuador's Electoral Disputes Tribunal (TCE) upheld González’s questionable disqualification from the upcoming provincial elections. She had run with the Citizen Revolution Movement, a party founded by former President Rafael Correa. A victim of lawfare, he now resides in Belgium, where he was given political asylum. Correa’s former vice-president, Jorge Glas, has been incarcerated since 2017 in a prosecution widely denounced as lawfare. Related: Colombia Threatens Its Caribbean Neighbor: Nicaragua The movement is Ecuador’s main opposition party, whose coalition won 67 of 151 National Assembly seats in the last election. The ruling right-wing party of President Daniel Noboa (a US citizen) won 66 seats. Conveniently for the right wing, the TCE “temporarily” suspended Citizen Revolution Movement candidates from running for public office. Another prominent opposition figure, Aquiles Álvarez, mayor of Guayaquil, Ecuador’s largest city, has been imprisoned since February 2026 on politically motivated charges after he scrutinized proven drug trafficking involving the Noboa family’s shipping company. His wife, Fiorella Ycaza, then came under investigation when she accused the government of political persecution. She is now running to succeed him as mayor. After her arrest, González protested: “We have reached an untenable situation… attacks on civil liberties and political persecution have become a permanent reality.” Her accusation extends well beyond Ecuador. Extreme lawfare in Venezuela In Venezuela, lawfare has extended beyond the manipulation of domestic judicial systems to the extraterritorial exercise of US criminal jurisdiction. US special forces kidnapped Venezuela’s lawful President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, National Assembly delegate Cilia Flores, last January 3. The imperial power claimed the prerogative to indict in absentia and seize a sitting head of state in an egregious exercise of naked judicial overreach. Alfred de Zayas, former UN independent expert on the promotion of a democratic and equitable international order (2012-2018), condemned the abduction as a violation of international law and an international crime. De Zayas lamented “the death of international order,” a characterization that is proving anything but hyperbolic. Acting President Delcy Rodríguez continues to govern under asphyxiating US sanctions, part of Washington's broader campaign of unilateral coercive measures that violate international law. Related: Did Venezuela Capitulate to Trump—or Choose Strategic Survival? Lawfare to appease anti-Cuba hardliners The obduracy of Cuba’s socialist government in resisting the mounting pressure for regime change from Washington provoked a new example of lawfare in October – this time from outside the country in question. Probably aimed at appeasing Florida’s Cuban gusanos, who have a profound hatred of Raúl Castro and his deceased brother Fidel, the state’s attorney general announced an arrest warrant against Raúl. Although Castro is unlikely to appear before a Miami court, the warrant was issued just two weeks before the US midterm elections and ahead of the annual UN vote condemning Washington's blockade of Cuba. Lawfare and “impunity-fare” in Honduras Trump’s blatant intervention in last year’s Honduran election swung it heavily in favor of the neoliberal candidate Nasry Asfura. Just two days before the election – in what might be called “impunity-fare” – Trump announced his intention to pardon former Honduran president Juan Orlando Hernández, a right-wing politician who was serving a 45-year US federal sentence for drug trafficking. Asfura has targeted opponents in the progressive Libre party while restoring the mano dura policies of previous neoliberal governments. Libre’s president of the National Congress until 2026, Luis Redondo, was the subject of an arrest warrant in October, along with 13 other prominent party members. Marlon Ochoa, Libre’s representative on the electoral tribunal, had challenged the questionable validity of Asfura’s election win. Ochoa fled the country in March, fearing for his life. Lawfare in Bolivia In Bolivia, allegations of lawfare arose after the right-wing government arrested Attorney General Roger Mariaca, who had been investigating figures associated with the political right. Shortly before his arrest, the US revoked his visa, accusing him of facilitating drug trafficking. Mariaca denounced the move as political interference and linked it to his investigation of Fernando Cerimedo, a former adviser to President Rodrigo Paz. Cerimedo has been dubbed Trump's “MAGA man” in Latin America. Meanwhile, former leftist president Evo Morales faces political persecution that appears to involve Cerimedo, backed by Washington. Related: Who Gets to Be a ‘Good’ Left-Wing Woman Leader? Brazil’s Lula vindicated The 2016 parliamentary coup that led to the impeachment and removal of Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff preceded the prosecution and imprisonment of Lula in 2018. Both instances are emblematic of the political use of legal proceedings against Brazil's left. Lula returned to office in 2023 and won reelection on October 25, defeating right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro. The apparent irony is that legal actions against Flávio’s father have also been dubbed “lawfare.” The key difference is that these involve genuine crimes. Further, Flávio fled to the US on October 27, reportedly with White House assistance, amid serious corruption allegations detailed by Globo , Brazil’s leading media conglomerate. US imperial playbook Progressive leaders who have lost power have faced not only defeat at the polls but a risk of subsequent imprisonment, sometimes resulting in lengthy sentences. Peru’s former president Pedro Castillo was arbitrarily imprisoned following his attempted dissolution of congress in December 2022. Argentina’s former president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner is under house arrest, unjustly convicted in a fraud case that led to a lifetime ban from public office in 2025. Taken together, these cases illustrate how the US imperial playbook can operate both before and after elections. Lawfare has become an essential tool in securing right-wing governments: Prior to the vote, scare the electorate into choosing a candidate favored by Trump who promises a firm hand against crime and “narcoterrorism.” After the vote, imprison political opponents to prevent them from undermining the government or mounting new electoral challenges. Shield political allies from prosecution, as Trump did with Juan Orlando Hernández, while denying such protection to opponents such as Luisa González. These tactics form part of a broader US interventionist strategy that includes sanctions, weaponized tariffs, and direct military force. Although intensified under Trump, the underlying imperial project has long enjoyed bipartisan support. However, after a streak of seven right-wing presidential election victories in Latin America, the outcome of Brazil’s contest has global implications – the rightward trajectory is reversible. According to Guillaume Long, former Ecuadorian foreign minister in the leftist Correa administration , Lula’s epic win “deals a major blow to…Trump’s increasingly interventionist agenda in the Western Hemisphere.” Nicaragua-based John Perry and US-based Roger D. Harris are both active with the Nicaragua Solidarity Coalition and the Task Force on the Americas .

articles.title: 100,000 California State Workers Struck Last Month
articles.author: Kari Thompson
articles.content: State workers went on a one-day unfair labor practice strike across California on October 21, with picket lines in Sacramento, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and other cities. They’re demanding better pay, affordable health care coverage, and flexibility to work from home. This was the first strike in the history of Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Local 1000, which represents about one hundred thousand government employees, ranging from accountants to custodians to nurses at state offices, hospitals, and prisons. They have been working without a contract since July 1. Some five thousand employees were excluded from striking. Governor Gavin Newsom’s “return-to-office” mandate went into effect this past summer. It requires workers to be in the office four days per week — even though workers report there isn’t enough space for all of them. Workers argue the return-to-office policy compounds the lack of pay increases. Being forced back into the office is “more than just a pay cut,” said Jonah Paul, who works for the Employment Development Department in Sacramento. ”It’s a huge reduction in quality of life. “Telework is a stopgap for a lot of problems our society is not willing to address,” Paul said: “The cost of childcare and insane commutes. Telework becomes a catch-all solution for a grueling life.” Zero Raise Last year, Local 1000 agreed to a pay freeze to help the state meet a budget shortfall. This summer, however, workers were supposed to see raises. But they got zilch. The union is asking for a 20 percent raise over three years to catch up, especially given increased state revenue over the past two years. Though Local 1000 and the state have met several times to negotiate a new contract, the union says CalHR, the bargaining representative for the state, has not been negotiating in good faith. It filed unfair labor practice charges with the state Public Employment Relations Board against CalHR for delaying negotiations and failing to respond to proposals. “When I first started working for the state ten years ago, for the most part CalHR would throw us a bone,” said Steward Giovanni Martinez, a state worker in Sacramento. “This is the worst bargaining cycle I’ve witnessed. They don’t want to budge on a lot of stuff. Newsom takes us for granted, and the people he’s appointed in CalHR are the same way.” Under previous leadership, the union kicked in $1 million to help Newsom fight a recall campaign in 2021. Members question why a governor they supported doesn’t have their backs now. Strike Schools Members of Local 1000 have been organizing over the past few months to increase membership numbers. Activists have been approaching nonmembers at their own worksites to ask them personally to join the union and calling others on the phone. Stewards did their best to increase communications across the membership, though they were hampered by limited updates from the official Bargaining Unit Negotiating Committee. Paul said that three years ago, the local offered “strike schools” to members, but these were more about discouraging members from planning for a strike. This time, he said, strike schools emphasized that the decision to strike was one for members to make, building membership numbers along with enthusiasm for walking out together. In a strike authorization vote held from September 9 to October 7, 96 percent voted “yes” to walk out. On the final day of the vote, the union held informational pickets to encourage participation in the vote. One picket happened to be next door to a building where Newsom was giving a speech. With just a half-hour’s notice, stewards and other union leaders managed to get members together to cover every entrance of the building and make enough noise that Newsom had to comment on it during his event. Despite this pressure from members, there was no last-minute deal to avert the strike, as happened ten years ago under Governor Jerry Brown. “For a lot of folks this is their first strike — this is mine,” Martinez said. “We didn’t want to walk off the job — we have a good relationship with our supervisors — but we had no choice.” World’s Fourth-Largest Economy Strike participation appeared strong, with thousands of workers joining rallies and marches in cities across the state. Striking workers in the state’s capitol shut down multiple blocks with a march from CalHR headquarters to the capitol building. “I was up on the truck with our president and a few other folks, leading people to different rally points,” said Emily Ingram, a Department of Education worker in Sacramento. “All you could see in every direction was more people. It was a pretty powerful feeling.” In Los Angeles, hundreds of workers rallied outside a state building. Arielle Mangabat-Lowe, who works at the Department of Toxic Substances Control, said she was surprised how many people showed up, after prior actions had only a few dozen participants. She reflected that it can be hard as an organizer to put so much work into the union without knowing whether other members will participate. But being with others at the strike rally boosted her spirits. “The state of California is a terrifying employer — it’s the world’s fourth-largest economy. We showed up today anyways,” she said. “It’s cool to feel like you have a voice, especially in these times.” “As someone who has been trying to get folks to join up, I think a lot of state workers are fired up,” said Martinez. “The energy is here. Where we go with it, that’s up to us as members and our leadership.” The union continued to pressure CalHR after the strike. On October 27, about twenty members disrupted a CalHR event in Sacramento, distributing flyers and shouting a message to the crowd demanding that the state stop intimidating members and bargain fairly. The two sides met for contract mediation on October 30, but they did not reach a deal. “We are continuing to prepare for another strike if needed,” Ingram said ahead of that meeting. articles.title: Sí, Se Puede
articles.author: Steve Appleford
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. At a vigil in downtown Los Angeles for Dolores Huerta, mourners gathered to remember the veteran labor organizer and civil rights activist with affection and awe. Behind the small crowd of dignitaries loomed a seven-story mural depicting Huerta as a young organizer, arms crossed, her face composed with quiet strength. There were tears and speeches from politicians and activists, along with repeated chants of the slogan Huerta popularized decades ago: “¡Sí, se puede!” (“Yes, we can!”). Admirers gathered at a vigil for the late labor organizer Dolores Huerta in downtown Los Angeles. Photo by Steve Appleford for Capital & Main. In the early evening dusk on Wednesday, hours after her death at age 96 from cancer, speakers recalled her role as a founding leader of what became the United Farm Workers union, and her decades of work advocating for immigrants’ rights, women’s rights and reproductive freedom. During the speeches, one biographical detail kept coming up: her size. At 5 feet tall, Huerta became a vibrant symbol of the power of an individual to make meaningful change. “She didn’t rely on her size. She relied on her inner strength,” her friend, California state Sen. María Elena Durazo, said in an interview a few days later. “How else do you convince farmworkers to take on agribusiness? She convinced them by showing them that they had power they never thought they had.” California State Sen. María Elena Durazo at a vigil for her friend, the late labor organizer Dolores Huerta, in downtown Los Angeles. Photo by Steve Appleford for Capital & Main. Huerta and César Chávez founded the National Farm Workers Association in 1962, seeking to organize California’s migrant farmworkers, who often labored in brutal conditions for extremely low wages. In 1965, the association joined Filipino farmworkers who had launched a strike in the grape-growing town of Delano. The ensuing strike and nationwide consumer boycott helped bring the plight of farmworkers to national attention and led to the creation of the UFW. “She was very good at getting people to think critically about the issues and enabling them to find their own agency in trying to affect change,” said Veronica Terriquez, director of the UCLA Chicano Studies Research Center. “She was an organizer, a strategist, and she also played a role in negotiating the contract. She will be known as one of the greatest civil rights leaders in United States history.” During her decades of protests, picket lines and labor actions, Huerta was arrested 22 times, and physically attacked by law enforcement and strikebreakers. Filmmaker and playwright Luis Valdez, who was on the front line of the movement in the 1960s, saw Huerta thrown off a Los Angeles loading dock and fall hard to the ground. “I thought she was hurt, but she popped up, climbed up on the dock and confronted her attackers,” Valdez said. In that first decade of organizing in the 1960s, the stakes were high for workers in the fields and orchards. It was backbreaking work amid the elements and toxic pesticides, often with no easy access to water and other basic needs. Related: Prison Reform: Wayne Kramer's Battle for Justice “Women were out there with no bathrooms in the fields,” Valdez said. “They had to squat behind the cars in order to do their business. That kind of disrespect already was endemic to the farmworkers’ life and agribusiness in general.” Lesser known was Huerta’s interest in the arts and how they might help the movement. She was instrumental in bringing Valdez’s El Teatro Campesino into the union in 1965, where it performed political sketches for workers in the fields and on the picket line, helping to communicate its message more effectively. “She saw right away the value of what theater could do for people,” said David Alvarado, director of the documentary American Pachuco: The Legend of Luis Valdez, released this year, which included an interview with Huerta. “Some of these farmworkers couldn’t read or write, so pamphlets and intellectual stump speeches about the value of political pressure could only go so far.” Valdez noted that Huerta was a listener to jazz records by John Coltrane and Miles Davis, and was a dancer and majorette early in life. “To some extent, those qualities remained part of her life — she was very much a majorette in that sense,” Valdez said, “the leader of the pack, the one who continued to stoke the fires of the movement.” The mural of Huerta, unveiled in April in time for Huerta’s 96th birthday and titled “Walking Into History,” was painted by Robert Vargas, who attended Wednesday’s vigil. Vargas has painted multiple murals around the city, depicting cultural heroes like pitcher Fernando Valenzuela with a trio of images overlooking Boyle Heights and rocker Eddie Van Halen in Hollywood. But his tribute to Huerta near East 4th and Main streets was especially personal. When she was in L.A., she would visit Vargas at the site, and they would have tacos together a few steps from the mural-in-progress. “When she spoke and gave you a call to action, you were ready to march, right then and there,” he said with a laugh. “At the same time, there was a humanity, a softness to her. And I got to know that person as well.” Related: What Can Dolores Huerta Teach Us About Movement-Building Now? In March, generations of admirers of the UFW were shaken by revelations, reported by The New York Times, that Chávez had sexually abused underage girls and women, including Huerta. The article documented multiple accusations of rape, and reported that Huerta bore two children from the assaults. Huerta was interviewed and quoted about the assaults, and said she had remained quiet to protect the movement. “She called me before the news broke,” Valdez said. “She wanted to let me know that this was coming out in The New York Times and that some of the allegations were true. It was a shock to me. She said it was going to be tough, but ‘I’ll have to face the music.’ She didn’t shy away.” One of Huerta’s later public appearances was at the Los Angeles premiere of American Pachuco in July. Just before the screening, she told Capital & Main of her work, “The whole idea about organizing was to get them to have the stamina and the courage to stand up for themselves.” Huerta taught that lesson to generations of activists, including Durazo, who first met the UFW founder while an organizer with UNITE HERE Local 11. They became close over the years, and occasionally differed in their opinions. “A good friend means that you have disagreements, and I had lots of disagreements with her,” Durazo said. “She would scold me and then a month later we’d be dancing on the floor at a wedding together.”anks for listenting. Capital & Main

articles.title: Data Centers Shape the 2026 Midterm Elections
articles.author: Marcus Baram
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In the final stretch of the 2026 midterm campaigns, the most potent climate issue in American politics arrived by delivery truck across the country. The average price of heating oil hit $6.23 a gallon for the week of Oct. 26, up from $3.60 a year earlier, according to the Energy Information Administration . At that price, filling a 250-gallon tank cost about $1,557 — roughly $657 more than the year before. As cold weather settled over the Northeast, Democrats turned that bill into an attack on Republican candidates. In New Hampshire, where about 43% of residents heat with oil, Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Chris Pappas said energy costs and heating oil prices were “the beginning and end of every conversation I’m having on the campaign trail.” That is the pattern across the closest races in this cycle. Energy is everywhere on the ballot — as heating oil, diesel, power bills and water — but almost always as a question of price. The argument over what actually powers the country — fossil fuels or renewables — surfaces mostly down-ballot, in low-profile contests for the commissions that regulate utilities and drilling. “If you talk to voters, they are upset about their energy bills and they’re upset about data centers,” Caroline Spears, executive director of Climate Cabinet, which backs climate-focused candidates in state and local races, told Capital & Main. “People want to hear from politicians about their plans on their energy bills and their plans on their data centers.” The consequences reach far beyond any one state. Control of the Senate will determine whether Congress revisits the clean energy tax credits Republicans rolled back in last year’s budget law. And the governors and regulators elected Tuesday will approve the gas plants, transmission lines and data center deals that shape the grid for decades to come. The U.S. Senate More than $191 million was spent on political ads referencing utility and energy bills in the first nine months of 2026, plus another $96.3 million from Oct. 1 to Oct. 16, according to AdImpact data analyzed by Climate Power , a Democratic-aligned advocacy group .In Maine, heating oil defined the final weeks of the race between Republican Sen. Susan Collins and her Democrat challenger Troy Jackson. Jackson said Mainers were paying 80% more for heating oil than a year earlier. Collins countered with an announcement: a release of 315,000 barrels from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve, which she and her counterpart, Sen. Angus King, had requested of President Donald Trump. Climate itself registers here, too: In the Environmental Voter Project’s polling of eight U.S. Senate battlegrounds, Maine had the highest share of voters naming it a top-three priority at 22%. In the farm belt, the price that matters is the cost of diesel. In Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek released a closing ad on fuel prices against Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson. Both candidates said data centers shouldn’t receive tax breaks — in a state that already gets more than 60% of its power from wind and solar. Kansas hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, yet Adam Hamilton built his challenge to Republican Sen. Roger Marshall around energy and utility costs, while Marshall said Kansans were “on fire” over data centers. High fuel and fertilizer prices have strained the farm economy in a state that generates roughly 50% of its electricity from wind. Data centers have scrambled the usual partisan lines. In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown branded Republican Sen. Jon Husted “the face of data centers,” and WinSenate, the country’s main Democratic Senate super PAC, ran an ad implying corrupt dealings between Husted and an energy company, though Husted was never charged. Kelcy Warren, executive chairman of the pipeline giant Energy Transfer, gave $3,500 to Husted’s campaign in late September. Related: Trump's Coal Revival Is Raising Electric Bills—and Voters Are Fighting Back In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers agree on little except data centers: Both back moratoriums in some form. El-Sayed’s framework would bar utilities from using data center demand to weaken Michigan’s clean-energy laws, while Rogers holds up to $250,000 in a Blackstone real estate trust that backs data centers. The climate stakes are concrete: Surging data center demand could trigger a provision in the state’s climate law that lets fossil fuel plants stay online during a capacity shortage. In Texas, where Democratic state Rep. James Talarico faces Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton for a critical U.S. Senate seat, the backdrop is Gov. Greg Abbott’s audit of every data center seeking to connect to the ERCOT grid — a review that won’t be finished until December, long after the midterm votes are cast. In Alaska, the fossil fuel question barely registers. Both Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola support oil and gas expansion, so the fight is over who will deliver it and who is to blame for Iran war-driven fuel costs. Sullivan has made the Alaska LNG pipeline, backed by a $54 billion South Korean investment, a centerpiece of his campaign. The Statehouses Thirty-six states will elect governors this November, and the nonpartisan Cook Political Report considers 12 of those contests competitive — including Alaska, Iowa, Georgia, Nevada, Ohio, Florida and Texas, where Republicans now hold the office. In 39 states, utility regulators are appointed by governors or legislatures rather than elected — which means many of those governors become energy policymakers whether they campaign on it or not. Climate surfaces more openly in Alaska’s overlooked governor’s race, where Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has pressed the state to address climate change and said it relies too heavily on natural gas — rare talk from an Alaska politician. Republicans Dave Bronson, Treg Taylor and Bernadette Wilson are also on the ballot. Nathaniel Stinnett, founder of the Environmental Voter Project, called Kreiss-Tomkins “probably the favorite” but said the race is “extraordinarily close.” In the group’s polling, 21% of likely Alaska voters identified climate as a top-three priority, second only to Maine. “I don’t wanna pretend like this is a climate election,” Stinnett said. “But certainly thousands and perhaps tens of thousands of Alaskans are going to vote with climate change top of mind.” In Nevada, the main climate focus is water. Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo sued the Trump administration over cuts to the state’s allotment of water from the Colorado River, and Arizona has since joined the suit. Nevada Conservation Voters gave Lombardo a C+ grade, crediting his support of clean energy while faulting his backing of fossil fuel projects. Because Democrats already control both chambers of the legislature, a win by his challenger, Attorney General Aaron Ford, would give the party a trifecta. Stinnett noted that Ford has talked up the clean energy transition in a state that “is kind of like the Saudi Arabia of solar energy, or it can be.” Kansas offers Republicans their best chance to flip a Democratic-held governorship. Republican Ty Masterson is more moderate on energy than many in his party, and both he and Democrat Cindy Holscher voted for a 2025 data center tax exemption. Holscher has since said she would freeze data center development until stronger guardrails are in place. Related: GOP Candidate Exploits Data Center Backlash to Hit Solar, Wind in Wisconsin Georgia’s open governor’s race between Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson will shape the state’s energy direction too — but the most direct fight over Georgia’s power sits further down the ballot. Legislatures may matter as much. Spears, the Climate Cabinet director, is focused on five states where Democrats could win full control — Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Arizona and Pennsylvania. “If they were a country, they’d be the world’s ninth largest climate polluter,” she said. “But 22 flipped seats stand between five trifectas and none.” Minnesota and Michigan both passed 100% clean energy laws the last time Democrats held full control. In Pennsylvania, where Republicans control the state Senate but not the House, Spears was blunt: “The Pennsylvania State Senate is where clean energy bills go to die.” The Regulators This is where fossil fuels and renewables actually collide. Spears called these “weird statewides” and said that as utility bills have become a defining issue, the culture war is “getting involved in utility elections as well.” Control of the Georgia Public Service Commission, which oversees Georgia Power, is on the ballot. Democrat Peter Hubbard, who won a special election last year, faces a rematch with Republican Fitz Johnson, while Republican Josh Tolbert and Democrat Shelia Edwards vie for an open seat. Republicans hold a 3-2 majority; if both Democrats win, Georgia would join Illinois’ commission as the nation’s only ones that are Democratic aligned. Hubbard argued the state is “oversubscribed on fossil fuels.” Johnson said data centers will pay their fair share because of protections he put in place. In Texas, the race for the Railroad Commission — which, despite its name, regulates an oil and gas industry that supplied nearly half the country’s oil last year — tightened after Republican Bo French drew widespread condemnation for a racist post on X. The Texas Oil and Gas Association, which represents ExxonMobil and Chevron, left him off its latest endorsement list. French has been bankrolled largely through PACs funded by billionaires Tim Dunn and Farris Wilks. His opponent, Democratic state Rep. Jon Rosenthal, is a former oil-field mechanical engineer. A Democrat hasn’t held a seat on the commission since 1994. Rosenthal traced the split to a rule backed by Jim Wright, the incumbent French ousted in the Republican primary, requiring liners for shallow oilfield waste pits so they don’t “leak noxious poison into the surrounding land and water, which I think most people think is a reasonable precaution.” Rosenthal, who said he has taken almost no money from oil and gas operators, has proposed banning industry donations to commissioners. “If we actually had ethical campaign finance laws, you wouldn’t want these people’s campaigns to be wholly or majorly funded by the people they’re supposed to regulate,” he said. “But that’s just how it is in Texas.” French did not respond to Capital & Main’s request for comment. In Arizona, Republicans Kevin Thompson and Ralph Heap face Democrats Clara Pratte and Jonathon Hill for two seats on the Corporation Commission as electricity provider the Arizona Public Service seeks a roughly 14% rate increase — and the decision is not expected until after the election. Heap’s platform, endorsed by right wing group Turning Point, reportedly centers on prioritizing coal. Even if both Democrats win, Republicans keep a majority, since only two of five seats are up. Colorado voters face the most literal version of the question. Amendment 82 would add a right to buy and sell natural gas to the state constitution and could limit state and local governments’ ability to enforce natural gas regulations. It needs 55% of the vote to pass. It is one of eight measures funded by the conservative group Advance Colorado — and the state’s own oil and gas industry opposed it, wary of upsetting its 2024 truce with Gov. Jared Polis. The Turnout Who shows up may matter as much as what’s on the ballot. A report from the Environmental Voter Project, which works to turn out voters who prioritize climate, found that as of Oct. 26, more than 3.7 million climate voters in 21 states had already cast early ballots, including more than 400,000 voting in a midterm for the first time. In every Senate battleground the group tracked, those voters were turning out faster than the electorate as a whole — often at twice the rate. In Georgia, 46.3% of climate voters had cast ballots by the time of the report, compared with 21.2% of all registered voters, Stinnett said. In Iowa, the figures were 22.8% and 9.5%. In Michigan and Nebraska, Stinnett said, the ratio was 2.5 to 1. “We often see that climate concerned voters are more likely to vote early than on Election Day,” he said. “But we’re not used to seeing margins like this.” His explanation: “Just because politicians aren’t talking about something doesn’t mean that voters aren’t concerned about it. Climate concerned Americans know how important these midterm elections are, and they ain’t gonna miss it come hell or high water.” Whether they are voting over a heating oil bill or a warming planet, the result lands in the same place. The senators elected this fall will decide what Washington does about clean energy, and the regulators will decide what gets built. The harder conversation starts after Nov. 3, Spears said, when the winners realize, “Oh, now I have to actually figure out what to do.” The bills will keep arriving long after the ballots are counted. Capital & Main
