articles.title: Iran-Contra at 40
articles.author: Christian Parenti
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. On Nov. 3, 1986, almost exactly 40 years ago, a Lebanese magazine called Ash Shiraa reported that the United States, with Israel as intermediary, had clandestinely sold millions of dollars of anti-aircraft missiles to Ayatollah Khomeini’s Iran in exchange for the release of six American hostages held by Hezbollah in Lebanon. It was one of a cascade of revelations about the covert workings of the American state that came to be known as the Iran-Contra affair. Forty years on, the state too often operates along similar lines, but for a rare moment in the late 1980s, there was real accountability. The first shock came about a month earlier, on Oct. 5, 1986, when the world awoke to the image of an American mercenary being led out of the jungle by two Nicaraguan soldiers. The new socialist government of Nicaragua had shot down a US airplane supplying weapons and ammunition to a CIA-backed counterrevolutionary army called the Contras. The only survivor of the crash was the man in the photo, Eugene Hasenfus. An experienced skydiver, Hasenfus was wearing a parachute and was close to the plane’s rear door, preparing to airdrop pallets of ammunition when the plane was hit. He immediately jumped. The pilot, co-pilot, and radio operator all died in the crash. Nicaraguan soldiers found Hasenfus huddled under his rain-soaked parachute. He was carrying identification that described him as an employee of Southern Air Transport, formerly owned by the CIA, and as a US military advisor working out of the Ilopango Air Force Base in El Salvador, where both the CIA and US military maintained a substantial presence. In the downed airframe’s wreckage were yet more documents linking the plane to the CIA and the Reagan White House. Hasenfus quickly confessed. Indeed, he was a CIA-contracted air-cargo specialist working on an agency-chartered transport plane delivering weapons to CIA-backed mercenaries; he had first worked for the agency almost two decades prior, as a cargo specialist with Air America in Laos and Vietnam. The Reagan administration denied everything, just as it would go on to deny the Ash Shiraa report about the arms transfers to Iran. But the stories wouldn’t go away. Competing journalists kept filling in details. Pundits started drawing comparisons to Watergate. On November 25, Attorney General Edwin Meese, hoping to get ahead of the Watergate comparison, held a news conference at which the administration copped to both crimes and surprised the world by admitting that the two stories were linked. “In the course of the arms transfers,” Meese explained, “certain monies which were received in the transaction between representatives of Israel and representatives of Iran were taken and made available to the forces in Central America, which are opposing the Sandinista government there.” The gamble failed. Public concern continued to grow. Iran-Contra offers a view into a type of elite power that is secret, illegal, and has major policy consequences. It exposed a species of nascently authoritarian statecraft that Peter Dale Scott would later call “deep politics.” The scandal also revealed much about American political and intellectual reluctance to confront such sub-rosa and anti-democratic maneuvering within the state apparatus. And it raised questions that have not yet been fully answered: what role do elite secrecy and illegality play in the reproduction of the current social order? In the case of Iran-Contra, the warmaking power that the US Constitution grants to Congress was illegally and secretly usurped by the executive branch, thus leading to a more violent and socially destructive foreign policy. To understand the scandal, it’s best to begin in Nicaragua in 1979, when a socialist revolution led by the Sandinista National Liberation Front overthrew the US-supported Somoza family dictatorship which had ruled Nicaragua since 1936. In power, the Marxist FSLN — known colloquially as the Sandinistas in honor of Augusto César Sandino, a populist rebel from the 1920s and ’30s — pursued a pragmatic mixed economy. Its five-member executive junta included two guerrilla leaders, but also prominent businessman Alfonso Robelo and liberal political dissident Violeta Chamorro, the widow of a martyred newspaper publisher. The Sandinistas nationalized many large businesses and most of the banks, pursued land reform, created a public-health system, and launched a massive and successful literacy campaign. Yet they left significant room for private enterprise and market competition. They never pursued a totally nationalized, centrally planned, Soviet-style economic model. Indeed, over half of Nicaraguan economic output remained in private hands. There was repression and censorship, to be sure, but at a level comparable to that of Leftand Right-wing regimes across the region in those days. Nonetheless, the US government refused to accept the loss of a client state and the establishment of any type of socialist experiment and immediately began subverting the project. When the Somoza regime fell, parts of its dreaded internal security apparatus fled into Honduras, where they were soon being equipped and trained by the CIA to run terrorist raids back in Nicaragua. At first, the US Congress supported this war to the tune of about $20 million a year (or about $74 million in current prices). However, the Contras’ methods were so barbarous — murder of civilians, widespread rape and torture, forced conscription — that their reputation as “freedom fighters” quickly eroded. In private, even Reagan called them vandals. In late 1982, Congress passed the Boland Amendment, placing legislative restrictions on aid to the Contras, which were further strengthened in 1984. Money for the Contra war was thus tightened, and the CIA’s management role was, at least on paper, considerably diminished. To legally comply with the Boland Amendment, formal control of the war passed from the CIA to the National Security Council, an inter-agency coordinating body within the White House. Key players in the NSC included the secretary of state, the secretary of defense, the director of the CIA, and the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. Below these honchos was a workforce of about 150, including a growing operations branch headed by Marine Corps Lt. Col. Oliver North. Reagan insiders acted as if this transfer of control from the CIA to the NSC were legal. Many in Congress saw it as profoundly unconstitutional. The legality of this arrangement was one of the scandal’s central conflicts. The Contra resupply effort now went “off books,” managed by a loose network of intelligence-connected individuals and private businesses, referred to by insiders as “the Enterprise.” To raise money, the Enterprise relied on contributions from rich anti-communists; foreign governments, such as Saudi Arabia; and the proceeds from illegal arms sales to the Islamic Republic of Iran. Most shocking of all, the Enterprise collaborated with known drug traffickers, who used some of their income from cocaine smuggling to help fund the Contras. Funds were handled through secret Swiss bank accounts. The actual work of supply and training was done by a network of small companies. Prominent among these were Southern Air Transport, formerly owned by the CIA but privatized in the early 1970s, and a mercenary company out of Alabama called Civilian Military Assistance. By the winter of 1987, four separate federal bodies were investigating the Enterprise. There was the “Tower Commission”— a three-member panel established on Nov. 26, 1986, by the executive branch and headed by Sen. John Tower (R-Texas). Second was the Independent Counsel’s investigation, appointed by the Department of Justice and headed by former judge Lawrence E. Walsh. The third investigation was really two linked and coordinated congressional committees: the House Select Committee to Investigate Covert Arms Transactions With Iran and the Senate Select Committee on Secret Military Assistance to Iran and the Nicaraguan Opposition. The fourth, and most important, probe was conducted by the so-called Kerry Committee, named for the 42-year-old junior senator from Massachusetts, John Kerry. A patrician Catholic and son of a diplomat, Kerry went to Groton, then Yale, joined the Navy, served in Vietnam, was wounded and decorated for valor in combat. Upon returning, he joined the radical peace group Vietnam Veterans Against the War. He marched in some of the group’s larger protests and, crucially, was part of the organization’s Winter Soldier Hearings, a grassroots, veteran-led investigation into American war crimes in Vietnam. As a former officer and social elite, Kerry lent the largely working-class, and frankly sometimes rather wild, VVAW a dose of credibility. Many in the establishment never forgave Kerry for these transgressions. As protest died down, Kerry earned his law degree from Boston College and launched his political career, arriving in the US Senate in 1985. Many Americans felt viscerally the importance of Kerry’s investigation into Contra drug running Kerry’s Senate investigation was formally known as the Senate Subcommittee on Terrorism, Narcotics, and International Operations. It dug deep into allegations of CIA-supported narcotics trafficking in the US homeland and, to the horror of many, found substantial evidence of drug smuggling by the Contras. Much of Iran-Contra was complicated: names, dates, front groups, agencies, meetings, more names, more dates. Plenty of ordinary people knew it was important, but found it tedious. However, the part about complicity with the cocaine trade wasn’t boring: it was simple and outrageous. You didn’t need to understand constitutional law to care about drug smuggling. By the late 1980s, America was awash in cheap, smokeable rock cocaine — the infamous “crack.” Addiction and violent crime were widespread. The US murder rate reached a second high in 1991 and has dropped considerably since then. American cities in the late 1980s were multiple times more violent than they are today. The country’s overdeveloped police and prison systems were then just gaining momentum. Many Americans felt viscerally the importance of Kerry’s investigation into Contra drug running. Nor was the public totally naive to the history of CIA drug connections. The story of agency cooperation with heroin smugglers in Southeast Asia during the Vietnam War was then almost 20 years old and well-documented. The US Senate’s Church Committee, in 1975 and 1976, had exposed that the CIA had experimented on American citizens with LSD and other drugs as part of its MK-Ultra program. CIA partnership with drug dealers was already part of the historical record and late-night man-cave pontificating all over America. Nevertheless, the allegations that American money was supporting the flow of illegal drugs into the United States still shocked and enraged the public. Kerry’s investigation began in April 1986, months before Hasenfus was shot down, as several papers, among them the Miami Herald and The Boston Globe, began reporting on allegations of drug smuggling by criminals involved with the Nicaraguan Contras. One source of these stories was a disgruntled American mercenary named Jack Terrell who had been employed by CMA,the Alabama mercenary company. Disgusted by what he witnessed, Terrell started talking to the media and Kerry’s research staff. None of the three other official investigations addressed governmentcondoned drug smuggling. In each of their final reports, a keyword search reveals that drugs, cocaine, and narcotics are mentioned only a few times in passing, with no sustained discussion or investigation. Even most of the mainstream media were openly hostile toward Kerry’s efforts. Newsweek was typical in calling the senator a “randy conspiracy buff.” Keep in mind that fear of ridicule and for one’s social standing are the most powerful forms of social control among the professional classes. At one congressional news conference in November 1987, an investigative journalist asked about governmentcondoned drug smuggling only to have The New York Times correspondent shout, “Why don’t you ask a serious question!” Important among the Kerry Committee’s trove of evidence was Oliver North’s personal diary, in which drug running was explicitly mentioned more than a dozen times. For example, in August, 1985, North noted the following: Honduran DC-6 which is being used for runs out of New Orleans is probably being used for drug runs into [the] US.” In July 1985, North described a call from retired Air Force Gen. Richard Secord — a crucial player in the Contra resupply effort — during which the two men discussed a specific arms purchase by the Contras. According to the diary, Secord told North that “14 [million] to finance [the arms purchase] came from drugs.” At no point did anyone involved in the NSC’s secret war inform the US Drug Enforcement Administration or any other law-enforcement agency that airplanes laden with illegal cocaine were inbound for the homeland. Not only did the Reagan NSC accept the fact that their Central-American mercenaries were running drugs, but at one point North even attempted to divert money from an anti-narcotics DEA operation to the Contras. The DEA officials involved refused, and two DEA agents testified before the Kerry Committee. The Kerry Committee’s final report, released in 1989, found that “senior US policymakers were not immune to the idea that drug money was a perfect solution to the Contras’ funding problems.” Thus, the committee concluded that, “in the name of supporting the Contras, we abandoned the responsibility our government has for protecting our citizens from all threats to their security and well-being.” Other investigations didn’t agree with Kerry. Even Democratic staff on the main Iran-Contra committee often refused to cooperate. As one Kerry investigator put it, “we had the White House and the CIA against us on one side and our colleagues in the Senate on the other.” National Public Radio and the major television networks didn’t broadcast Kerry’s hearings. Public exposure was limited. Respectable opinion avoided Kerry’s findings. Nonetheless, in 1998, the CIA’s own Office of the Inspector General confirmed the Kerry Committee’s core findings that the agency had known and ignored that the Contras were deeply involved in cocaine trafficking. As the report put it, the CIA worked with at least “six companies that had been owned and operated by convicted or suspected drug traffickers and were linked to the Contras.” This connivance violated the CIA’s legal obligation to report crimes up the chain of command. The agency’s regulations stated that any violation of US criminal law “by CIA officers and employees, or relating to CIA affairs, shall be reported immediately by an employee to the Inspector General, who shall inform the General Counsel.” That was not done. Furthermore, the OIG found that the agency hid evidence to mislead Congress. The defining spectacle of the Iran-Contra affair came in the summer of 1987, when the House and Senate Joint Select committees held 40 days of public hearings. Though dismissed by many as an elaborate whitewash, the hearings did reveal significant illegal activity. Key players were hauled before the cameras and interrogated. Reams of incriminating documents were quoted and entered into the record. But the hearings also, at times conspicuously, avoided evidence of the most controversial crimes, such as drug smuggling. Enforcing these boundaries was the committee chairman, Sen. Daniel Inouye of Hawaii (and a World War II hero). A second-generation Japanese-American, Inouye had served in the all-Nisei 442nd Regiment of the US Army — the most decorated American unit in the war. As an infantry lieutenant, Inouye lost his right arm fighting the Germans in Italy. During convalescence, he befriended a wounded Bob Dole, who later became a senator from Kansas and a perennial Republican presidential candidate. The instinct of men like Inouye was: my country, right or wrong. Inouye was made chairman because of his diplomacy, perfect etiquette, and previous experience serving on the Senate Watergate Committee. Yet it was hard not to feel that Inouye had also been cast in this role because of who he was: a Japanese-American who literally gave his right arm for his country, even as his country forcibly incarcerated 120,000 innocent Japanese- Americans. Inouye, in short, was the embodiment of forbearance, equanimity, and forgiveness. His mere presence seemed to say: don’t overreact. As chairman, Inouye had the power to shut down any line of questioning, and used that power to avoid inflammatory revelations. Indeed, Inouye appeared to want to expose as much painful information as needed to restore faith in the system, but no more than that. For example, when news broke that Oliver North and other members of the Enterprise had drawn up contingency plans for an emergency suspension of the Constitution — in case of, among other things, a US invasion of Central America — Rep. Jack Brooks (D-Texas) had the temerity to question North about these secret “plans for the continuity of government.” North, his lawyer, and several senators sitting around Inouye looked visibly stressed. The chairman, ever the diplomat, shut down the questioning with: “May I most respectfully request that that matter not be touched upon at this stage. If we wish to get into this, I’m certain arrangements can be made for an executive session.” A seemingly entranced Brooks complied. Yet even Inouye acknowledged that there existed “a shadowy government with its own air force, its own navy, its own fundraising mechanism, and the ability to pursue its own ideas of the national interest, free from all checks and balances, and free from the law itself.” As important as Kerry’s exposé was the surprisingly aggressive nature of the Independent Counsel’s investigation and then prosecutions. Lawrence E. Walsh was an old-school establishment Republican and loyal party insider. He had been a Wall Street lawyer and then a judge. Already 74 years old and with an ailing wife when first appointed, Walsh was initially dismissed by many as part of the cover-up. But Walsh put the Constitution above party. He went where the evidence led, even when that meant prosecuting top-level Reagan administration insiders. Both the Reagan and Bush administrations fought with and sabotaged Walsh at every step. But he carried on. Ultimately, Walsh brought criminal charges against 14 individuals, and secured 11 convictions. Both Oliver North and National Security Adviser John Poindexter were convicted. Many of the convictions were overturned on appeal because of technicalities about certain types of legal immunity having created inadmissible evidence. Walsh was set to prosecute yet more suspects, including former Secretary of Defense Caspar Weinberger, but on Dec. 24, 1992, President George H. W. Bush issued pardons vacating one conviction, three guilty pleas, and two pending cases. The pardons crippled Walsh’s efforts. His final report was published in August 1993, and though it avoided CIA complicity in drug smuggling, it did establish that both Reagan and Bush knew “that high-ranking administration officials violated laws” and destroyed evidence as part of “a concerted effort to deceive Congress and the public.” “Iran-Contra was, in short, the essence of anti-democratic, authoritarian politics. Just as amazing as Iran-Contra’s season of sunlight was how quickly the media and public seemed to forget most of the basic history. A decade after Hasenfus had been led out of the jungle, The San Jose Mercury News reporter Gary Webb “broke” the story of CIA complicity in drug smuggling all over again. For those of us who had followed the Kerry Committee, the late 1990s surge of attention to CIA complicity in drug trafficking was welcome but also depressing. Everyone was outraged, all over again, including members of Congress who acted as if there weren’t already a 1,000-page report on this very question. The American urge to forget is deep; so, too, is the desire to be scandalized, again and again. During the second season of outrage, the Kerry Committee was rarely mentioned. Predictably, Gary Webb was soon attacked in the same fashion Kerry had been. The press turned on Webb, the intellectuals and liberal professionals abandoned him. Before long, it was only angry black people from drug-ravaged neighborhoods telling the truth about the government’s role in abetting the drug trade. More often than not, they were treated as crazy for pointing out facts that had been documented by the US Senate. The gatekeepers of national discourse, the condescending chattering classes, were hostile and had moved on. Webb eventually committed suicide. In the end, the Iran-Contra investigations played a strangely dialectical role: they exposed real wrongdoing; but three of the four investigations also functioned as elaborate theatrical concealments of the more serious crimes uncovered by the Kerry Committee, foremost among those CIA-tolerated drug smuggling. So, too, the effects of the spectacle were contradictory. On the one hand, cynicism deepened. But on the other hand, liberal democracy’s immune system against tyranny kicked in, and the political cancer of undemocratic secret government was put, at least momentarily, into remission. During Iran-Contra, Congress at first funded a covert war, then cut off such funding. Both Congress’s funding and defunding of the war were fully legal powers of the legislative branch under the US Constitution — for example, the taxing and spending and war powers clauses. Outrageously, the executive branch defied Congress to secretly and illegally continue an unpopular war. And as part of that effort, it allowed addictive drugs to flood the country. Iran-Contra was, in short, the essence of anti-democratic, authoritarian politics. Iran-Contra showed that the machinery of liberal democracy still, almost, had the capacity to defend and reproduce itself. Sadly, there is reason to fear thatduring the intervening 40 years, democratic government’s ability to impose accountability upon elite covert politics has only weakened, and that all we have left is the outrage. articles.title: The US Electorate Is Permanently Mobilized and Unable to Move
articles.author: Corey Robin
articles.content: Six theses on the midterm elections: Early voting tallies are through the roof . If the patterns continue, turnout is expected to match that of the midterm elections in 2018 , which saw the highest turnout rate in a midterm election since 1914. This comes in the wake of turnout for the 2020 election, which was the highest since 1900. Turnout in the 2026 midterm election is supposed to be especially high among black, Latino, and independent voters. Despite nearly a decade’s worth of record turnout, the electorate remains still roughly evenly divided, oscillating around the 50/50 mark. Even when one party manages to seize control of all the elected branches of the federal government, it doesn’t make a lasting dent in the divided nature of the electorate. Even when that party manages to push through major innovations in governance and legislation, it doesn’t fundamentally reshape the electorate. We’re as divided or polarized (take your pick) as we have been since the second term of Barack Obama. Unable to fundamentally reshape the electorate, politicians and parties have also not been able to permanently reshape the government, at least not yet. Donald Trump has certainly done monumental damage to the American state, bringing levels of corruption and administrative malfeasance and downsizing that indicate a long-term hit to administrative capacity. Yet it won’t be until a successor from the opposition comes along that we’ll truly see what was done and what can be undone or remade. What we do know is that Trump 1 wasn’t able to stop the dramatic innovations of Joe Biden and that Biden’s innovations had virtually no effect on Trump 2. Despite deep grumblings of an epically dissatisfied electorate, entire sectors of the political economy and social world remain on track to continue the path they’ve been on. Climate change is virtually off the table as a topic of policy and politics. Wealth inequality is worse today than it was ten years ago. Neither party has any kind of plan or even promise for artificial intelligence. The markets continue leading us to the precipice of irrational exuberance. Despite the best efforts of one party to suppress the vote, and both parties to gerrymander the vote, the electorate refuses to be bowed or cowed by the state. All the traditional mechanisms of voter suppression, while unconstitutional and thus to be resisted at every step, and effective around the edges, don’t seem able to dislodge the electorate itself. We have then a puzzle. On the one hand, an electorate that is more mobilized than it’s been in a century, and not just episodically mobilized but permanently mobilized. On the other hand, we have what I called, in an article about Max Weber for The New Yorker back in 2020, “the stuckness” of contemporary politics, in which “the particles of academic and political life have slowed to a halt” and “all that was air has become solid.” That’s where we are — permanently mobilized and unable to move — and like Weber, we long for eruptions and charismatic leaders to get us out of that stuckness. But whether the way out lies in electoral politics, non-reformist reforms, or more radical options, each of them will involve the long and patient creation of organizations that can sustain leftist politics over the long haul, not the episodic gestures and eruptions that Anton Jäger has so rightly marked as the emblems of our hyperpolitical age . Again, regardless of the path, from reform to radicalism and beyond, there’s still no alternative to that other Weberian metaphor, so beloved of centrists and liberals alike, yet so pertinent to the Left right now: the slow boring of hard boards. The good news is that there is a younger generation, perhaps two, that seems to get this, and is working toward the future, with no expectation of easy victories or quick solutions — and without the melancholy and grating pessimism, and the clichés, god, the clichés (pessimism of the intellect, optimism of the will, barf) of the older generations. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Democratic Congress
articles.author: Jack Rasmus
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The French have a saying: “Plus ca change; rien ca change”. Translated it means ‘everything changes, nothing changes’; or, depending on your French, ‘everything changes but everything remains the same’. That likely describes the current midterm 2026 US elections. Whichever party takes the House or the Senate, the policies of recent years will not change much. US foreign policy under Trump’s last two years will remain on its current disaster trajectory. And the domestic policy excesses of the past two years will remain mostly intact. Trump Will Simply Ignore the House Should the Democrats retake the House, Trump will continue his imperialist wars and regime change operations. That includes ignoring any renewed impeachment proceedings or House tepid War Powers resolutions. He will simply ignore them, should they even occur. For reasons explained shortly, don’t hold your breath for anything significant coming out of a Democrat House in either regard the next two years. Moreover, a Democrat House will continue as it has in the past supporting Israel and may even increase US support for the Ukraine war. And it will grant Trump much of his requests for increasing Pentagon spending in 2027-28. So ‘rien ca change’ here in foreign policy, folks. So far as domestic US policy is concerned, he doesn’t need US House support for any new major initiatives. Trump has already achieved his main domestic policy objectives in 2025-26—i.e. getting his $5 trillion corporate-investor tax cuts passed; $191 billion for thousands of more immigration police, ICE agents, and ‘detention’ centers; cuts of more than a trillion dollars in Medicaid, ACA and other health care spending; and 426,000 US federal workers laid off or driven from their jobs in the past eighteen months. Nor does Trump need Democrat House support to continue to pursue his tariffs policy. He may have been forced by the Supreme Court to return some of the $288 billion in tariffs revenue but he can easily find a legal workaround by relying on other past legislation. Congress has been, and will remain, a non-player in tariff policy. Not least, a Democrat House (and Senate) will go along with funding most of Trump’s requested $400 billion increase in Pentagon spending, which is already at $1.1 trillion and rising. And there’s more for other defense spending categories like Veterans benefits, CIA, Homeland Security, Nuclear Weapons development, secret weapons projects, and defense spending’s share of interest on the national debt. The Democrats will more than go along to refund the US military’s current seriously depleted stock of missiles inventory, loss of equipment in the Iran conflict, new offshore military base development, and a program of crash funding to develop next generation AI enabled autonomous weapons, drones and hypersonic missiles—in all of which categories the US now lags behind Russia and China. In short, Trump does not need a Democrat controlled US House to pass new legislation for him in 2027-28. And he knows the Dems will give him most of what he wants in new defense spending. Related: The American Empire Is Running Out of Money Impeachment as Political Marketing Then there’s the hot issue of a Democrat controlled US House impeaching him. Will they or won’t they? Trump doesn’t care. As the saying goes: ‘Been there, done that’. He weathered two prior impeachment efforts. It’s doubtful he cares about a third. Here’s why: First, it’s only 50-50 the Democrats will even bother to impeach him. They’ll act like they are going to. Lots of talk. Committee hearings. But bringing a vote will be drag and delay until late in 2027. And by late 2027, with only a year left in Trump’s term, the US House Dem leadership—Hakeem Jeffries and the oligarchs who run the party’s central committee—will argue to their party ranks in the House that he’ll be gone in twelve months anyway, so it’s a waste of time to impeach. They’ll point to the Senate where the Dems—who at best may have no more than a two seat majority—will argue they don’t have the votes to convict Trump and that he’ll be gone in a year. The Democrats will use the threat of impeachment to keep the issues justifying it before the public the next two years—i.e. his illegal wars, his personal financial corruption, violations of the US Constitution, abuse of executive authority, destruction of democratic norms, etc. The talk of impeaching is politically more useful than the act, Dem leaders will argue. In recent decades impeachment has become a political marketing tool of the parties and not really a constitutional means for removing a president. In that latter regard it has clearly failed as a provision of the US Constitution. James Madison and Thomas Jefferson would no doubt agree. They warned about it, and how what they called ‘factions’—aka parties—controlled by a small group or one person like Trump would undermine the US Constitution’s idea of institutional ‘checks and balances’. More likely than pushing to impeach Trump, Jeffries & Company will throw a bone to their Democrat party rank and file and instead impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. That would help put a Trump impeachment on a back burner and create the delay to put off impeaching Trump in his last months in office. Trump might even favor a Hegseth impeachment and removal. It would give him cover to extricate from the Iran conflict. Blame Hegseth for the fiasco as the architect who lied to him (Trump) and throw him ‘under the political bus’. In Trump typical fashion, he’ll then blame the Democrats for the Hegseth removal. In summary, there are good reasons to argue Trump will just not care all that much if the Democrats take the House. It won’t have any appreciable impact on his policies domestic or foreign, regardless of the Democrat vote margin. And an impeachment vote by the House won’t get very far in the Senate, he’ll conclude. So let ‘em rant and rave about impeachment. It’s just political theater. He might care more if the Democrats achieve a significant majority of 60 seats in the Senate. But a one or two seat Democrat Senate majority—which is the best case outcome for the Democrats in the election—will never result in an impeachment trial, let alone a conviction, and Trump knows it. There’ll be no ‘blue wave’ in the Senate election. The numbers and polls just don’t support it. The mainstream media—CNN in this case—predicts a 52-48 Democrat majority in the Senate. In other words, a barely significant political pendulum swing… once again. If Trump was all that concerned about losing Congress, he would have campaigned more aggressively on behalf of Republican candidates in recent weeks. He campaigned very little for Republican House candidates. And only occasionally went out and campaigned for Senate members of his party. He just doesn’t care about the party either. Trump may not even care that if the Senate held a trial following the unlikely event of House impeachment. Holding a trial in the Senate is one thing; voting to convict is another thing. It is extremely unlikely there will ever be either in the Senate, especially with a 52-48 Democrat majority. He knows that too. In short, the odds of the House impeaching Trump are low; of the Senate taking it to trial even lower; and voting a conviction virtually nil! So Trump may not care all that much what happens on November 3, 2026. He’ll just stonewall away after the election pursuing his disastrous foreign wars and policies. And blame everyone else for the failures. And should the AI boom implode and the real economy contract—which is beginning to appear increasingly likely in recent weeks—he’ll just find someone else to blame as well. Probably Scott Bessent, whose departure would be no great intellectual loss for the country in any event. Notwithstanding all this, what’s the likely actual outcome of the midterm elections in the US House and Senate on November 3? The mainstream media-CNN forecast is optimistic for the Democrats. Mainstream media polling has historically in recent years over-estimated outcomes in favor of the Democrats. And it will likely repeat that error shortly. Likely US House of Representatives Election Outcomes If one were to believe mainstream media, it’s going to be a ‘blue wave’ in the House on November 3. CNN’s latest polling predicts the current 218 to 214 margin favoring Republicans will result in a final 237 Democrats to 198 Republicans seat distribution. But that’s a Democrat gain of only 23 net seats over their current 214! Hardly a blue wave. Moreover, 23 net seats may be the best case scenario not the most likely. CNN polling shows only 224 seats now ‘leaning Democrat’. That’s only 10 more than they now have. Most pundits agree only 40-45 seats in the House are ‘in play’, as they say. It is a sad state of American Democracy today that no more than 10% of the 435 House seats are ever up for change. That’s because of the recent decades of gerrymandering of the US House of Representatives by BOTH parties. Republicans and Democrats alike have ensconced themselves into safe seats by cleverly redefining House districts. They then financially and legally gang up on anyone who dares to run as an independent or from any other party. Ballot denial of all challengers is a game both play. The American voting public has been institutionally disenfranchised by the extreme gerrymandering in recent years—all of which has been endorsed and legitimized by the US Supreme Court. Related: Fed Rates, US Treasury Market & Crisis of Empire Likely US Senate 2026 Election As difficult as it is for a large majority shift to occur in the US House, it’s even more difficult in the US Senate. Party majority swings in the Senate are typically no more than 2 or 3 seats at most. That’s likely to be the case in 2026 as well. With such small majorities, it doesn’t take more than a couple party crossovers to thwart a meaningful policy change when the ‘out’ party regains a temporary small majority in the Senate. A good example of how a few crossover votes thwart change in the Senate is what occurred under the Biden administration when just two Democrat Senators, Joe Manchin and Kyrsten Sinema, blocked all attempts to reverse Trump’s $4 trillion 2018 tax cut handout to corporations and investors. Biden and Democrat party leadership in the Senate did little to pressure them to back off from blocking tax reform at the time. Trump’s 2018 tax cuts were left in place and thereafter expanded and made permanent in 2025. That cost the US Treasury another $5 trillion, according to the Congressional Budget Office. Here’s why little will change in the Senate election, apart from maybe a couple seat Democrat majority at best: The 2026 Senate election involves 35 of its 100 seats. No more than 9 seats are actually competitive and flippable. These include the 7 Republican Senate seats in the following states: Alaska, Texas, Ohio, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina, Maine. Competitive races where Democrats hold seats that they may lose involve Michigan and Georgia. So only 9 of the 35 seats are competitive. Once again, only about 10% of the Senate’s 100 seats are up for change in the election, much like the House’s 40-45. To get a majority in the Senate, Democrats must hold onto seats in Michigan and Georgia which are ‘in play’ and competitive, according to polls, and must win a net of four of the seven contested Republican Senate seats. A net of four seats would give them a total 51 seat majority in the Senate. Polling shows a solid Democrat lead for in Georgia and a narrower lead in Michigan as challenger Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive, contends with a Republican opponent. The outcome of the Michigan race race is less certain than Georgia but both are a must ‘hold’ for the Democrats. El-Sayed has faced significant Democrat party, corporate oligarch and Zionist opposition as well as unfriendly mainstream media propaganda. Trump has also gone public strongly opposing El-Sayed. Even El-Sayed’s defeated Democrat party primary competitor has jumped the Dem party ship and endorsed El-Sayed’s Republican opponent. More than $400 million reportedly has been spent thus far on the Michigan race—much of it from business and Zionist sources, domestic and foreign, and much spent against El-Sayed. The final spending will likely be closer to $1 billion than to $500 million once all the campaign Ad spending is counted. While El-Sayed has a small lead in the polls, the mountain of money committed against him by Zionist and business interests leaves the race too close to call. But the Democrats must win Michigan (and Georgia) or their numbers for taking back the Senate collapse. In Georgia, incumbent Democrat Ossof appears to have a commanding lead for re-election. So that’s one definite Democrat and one uncertain in Michigan. However, the Democrats must win both. That leaves the remaining seven Republican held seats in play. To achieve a net four seat margin in these seven races, the Democrats must win at least six of the seven seats. That will give them CNN’s predicted 52 seat majority in the Senate. That’s six of the following seven seats: Alaska, Texas, Ohio, Kansas, North Carolina, Iowa and Maine. The most likely Democrat wins are Maine, North Carolina, Kansas and maybe Ohio. That’s an optimistic four. They need two more from the remaining three: Texas, Alaska and Iowa. That’s a daunting task. Iowa is highly unlikely given its decades long history and the latest tight polling. That means the Democrats must take both Alaska and Texas. That’s an uphill battle for the following reasons: Alaska is interesting in that the Trump administration is already preparing to intervene and overturn the election there should the Democrat Senate candidate, Mary Peltola, win against Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan. Another third party candidate also named Dan Sullivan is apparently on the ballot. Trump administration argues it was a tactical ploy by the Democrats to put the second Dan Sullivan on the ballot. Should Republican Sullivan lose, Trump forces will argue it was interference and campaign fraud. Courts have already ruled Sullivan #2 has as much right as a citizen to run as Republican Sullivan. But this won’t stop legal action by Trump to negate the Alaska election and demand a re-run. The second must win is Texas, which has not elected a Democrat Senator since 1988. Apart from the El-Sayed Michigan race, mountains of oligarch money has poured into the Texas race as well. More than $500 million has been spent to date. That’s more than $1 billion in just two states: Michigan and Texas. (And another $450 million in Ohio). Can anyone imagine this happening without the Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizen United case that ruled corporations were people and that their spending money on elections was a form of ‘free speech’ under the US Constitution! In short, the Democrats must also take both Texas and Alaska in order to win even a narrow 52 majority in the Senate. And if by chance Democrat Talarico wins in Texas, then one can be sure the outcome of who controls the Senate will be determined by a long drawn-out court fight over the ‘two Sullivan’s’ issue in the Alaska race. And no seating of an Alaskan Senator means one less seat for the Democrats’ pursuit of a Senate majority. What this all means is that Trump has little to fear from the Senate in the highly unlikely event of a House impeachment vote—i.e. a trial or conviction—with a mere 51 or even 52 seat majority. One suspects, therefore, he probably cares little about what happens in the 2026 midterm election in either House of Congress. Conclusions So the immediate post election scenario is not some kind of severe constitutional crisis of the system a la January 2021, as some commentaries and pundits are predicting. There’s little chance of impeachment, and no chance of trial in the Senate. Therefore there’ll be more of the same Trump foreign policies of wars, more budget deficit busting war spending, more regime change operations (especially against weak countries like Cuba in the western hemisphere), and more aggressive action toward Canada and Greenland. Trump will not try to overturn or generally subvert the midterm elections process, impound ballots or engage in other constitutionally challenging tactics, except possibly in Alaska. He doesn’t need to. He’ll just ignore the US House election outcome and, worst case, tie up the Senate election results in the courts. He doesn’t care about getting House support to introduce new domestic legislation. And he’ll just ignore any Congressional attempts to interfere with his war mongering foreign policies. 2026 is therefore just another ‘Ho-Hum’ US election that will change little of any real consequence for the American public. It will prove just another example of the bi-annual ‘shell game’ where one wing of the Corporate Party of America—the Democrats—takes over from the other Republican wing. Followed by another similar token switch back to Republicans in 2028 when more Democrat Senate seats are up for re-election than Republican and another couple dozen gerrymandered House seats flip flop again. Election 2026 is just Déjà vu. Another ‘rien ca change’. Just as it has been for the past three decades at least. And mainstream media dares call it American Democracy?

articles.title: Captain Picard Was a Socialist, and So Was Patrick Stewart
articles.author: Alexander Deley
articles.content: For those of us who grew up watching Star Trek: The Next Generation , Patrick Stewart’s death last week was an enormous loss. Stewart was an actor of extraordinary talent, commanding every scene he appeared in while bringing emotional depth to even the most imposing characters. Equally comfortable with Shakespearean tragedy, science fiction, and comedy, Stewart could do it all. There was also something about his premature baldness that aged him — adding to his already impressive natural gravitas — but also gave him an ageless quality over the decades. Whether he was performing Shakespeare onstage or appearing in sci-fi shlock like the naked-space-vampire thriller Lifeforce (1985), he always fully embodied the characters that he played. Best remembered for his portrayal of Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation , Stewart was also something exceedingly rare among Hollywood’s biggest stars: an unapologetic, lifelong socialist. He never hesitated to make his political convictions known, even among the industry’s wealthy elite: “There’s nothing more fun than being at a dinner party in Beverly Hills, surrounded by elegant people, and telling them you’re a socialist.” A Socialist from the Start Much of Stewart’s radical political perspective emerged at an early age. Born in 1940, he grew up poor in Yorkshire, England, the youngest of three brothers. Stewart’s mother worked in a textile factory, while his father worked several working-class jobs, including as a day laborer and postman, never coming to terms with the post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) he suffered from after his experiences during World War II. Stewart’s father would often subject his wife to domestic violence. Witnessing his mother’s exploitation at work and abuse at home profoundly shaped Stewart’s politics. Rather than accepting these injustices as inevitable, he committed himself to fighting them. Stewart said he became a socialist at the age of five. Later in life, he became an outspoken campaigner against domestic violence, drawing on the experiences that had so blighted his childhood: I’ve been a witness to unfairness in society all my life. To the conditions under which my mother worked all her life, working in an industrial weaving shed in the north of England. And it has been this feature of unfairness that has motivated me in all of my political thinking. Stewart also discovered from a young age, with the encouragement of his grammar school English teacher, that he had a wonderful talent for acting. Indeed, at the age of ten, that very teacher gave the young Patrick a copy of Macbeth and told him to get up on stage and perform. Stewart was a natural. He continued to act throughout his school career, often working alongside friend Brian Blessed, who would also go on to an impressive dramatic career of his own. Stewart and Blessed later received grants to attend the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School. Stewart was reportedly the first person who was neither a graduate of Oxford nor Cambridge to receive a grant from West Riding Council. Stewart began his professional career in 1959 with a production of Cyrano de Bergerac in Bristol. In 1966, he joined the Royal Shakespeare Company, where he worked alongside actors such as Ben Kingsley. In 1967, he also made his on-screen debut, landing a one-off bit part in the long-running UK soap opera Coronation Street . He subsequently appeared in Shakespearean plays and BBC dramas, including turns playing Vladimir Lenin in Fall of Eagles (1974) and the KGB mastermind Karla in the critically acclaimed adaptations of John le Carré’s Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy (1979) and Smiley’s People (1982). It also paved the way for a number of bit parts in films. These included John Boorman’s Excalibur (1981) and David Lynch’s Dune (1984), where his character Gurney Halleck memorably charges into battle cradling a pug. Even as his screen career developed, Stewart maintained a deep commitment to the theater, encouraged by his lifelong friend and fellow Shakespearean powerhouse actor, Ian McKellen. Indeed, Stewart’s longtime connection to the theater and to Shakespeare proved to be key in his landing the role that would propel him to global fame. The Making of Captain Picard When Stewart was cast as Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation (1987–1994), he drew on his years of Shakespearean training to develop the starship captain. As he put it, “There is a formality to the way they speak and comport themselves that reminds me of numerous Shakespearean situations I’d been in onstage. I should play Jean-Luc, I realized, as if he were a character in Henry IV , which is about brave men.” This proved to be a stroke of genius, with Picard immediately becoming a fan favorite. Picard’s assured and wise but commanding demeanor alongside his philosophical bent proved to be the very ideal representation of who one would want to have exploring the cosmos on behalf of humanity. The show is considered by many to be the greatest iteration of Star Trek , and it is likely the version that hewed most firmly to series creator Gene Roddenberry’s famously left-wing politics, politics shared by Stewart. His singular performance helped make the show a success, and it made Stewart a household name and transformed him into an international star. To viewers like me, who grew up watching The Next Generation , Picard represented the ideal father figure, something he himself never had. Yes, Picard had a quiet authority — Stewart said his own father could command any room he walked into — but Picard was also a man of deep kindness, intelligence, and compassion with a strong aversion to violence. His mission was one of peace, and though the USS Enterprise often found itself in peril, Picard was almost always able to negotiate a nonviolent way out. Picard embodied a vision of authority based not on domination but on cooperation, reason, and mutual respect. It was a vision compatible with Stewart’s socialism — a commitment to humanity over the barbarism of domination and violence. The Humanity of Jean-Luc Picard Perhaps Stewart’s most powerful exploration of these themes came in the two-part Next Generation episode “The Best of Both Worlds.” Over the course of the two episodes, the Enterprise encounters the Borg, a monstrous cybernetic collective that absorbs other civilizations into a single hive mind — an unsettling vision of the individual entirely subordinated to a larger power. Captured and assimilated by the Borg, Picard is eventually rescued by his crew. But the experience leaves him profoundly traumatized, forcing him to struggle with the lasting consequences of having his humanity stripped away. Throughout the rest of the series, whenever Picard has further encounters with the Borg, he must struggle with his own belief in the sanctity of all life in the universe, versus resentment and the desire for revenge. Stewart’s portrayal of Picard’s anguish may have drawn on his own experience of childhood trauma growing up in a violent household — he had certainly spoken about the lasting psychological damage caused by his father’s abuse. Picard’s subsequent encounters with the Borg repeatedly tested his commitment to compassion over revenge. His struggle to resist violence, even against those who had harmed him, remains one of the series’ most affecting expressions of its humanistic ideals. Stewart also became a fierce defender of science fiction as a genre, recognizing its ability to explore complex moral, ethical, and philosophical questions. He once reportedly walked off a Good Morning America promotional appearance after learning that producers intended to ridicule the show and science fiction as a whole. The series of course was wildly successful, not only reviving the Star Trek franchise but spawning four feature films, each time with Stewart reprising his starring role. This respect for science fiction and genre entertainment was also probably what helped guide Stewart to his other most iconic role: Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film franchise. Beginning with the Bryan Singer adaptation X-Men (2000), Stewart played the psychically powered founder of, and mentor to, the X-Men across several films. Working alongside old friend Ian McKellen (in the roll of the antagonist of the series, Magneto), the films, much like the comics they were based on, explored the conflicting philosophies of the two men in a wider metaphor for the civil rights movement. Stewart’s Xavier sought equality and coexistence between humans and superpowered mutants, while McKellen’s Magneto favored a more militant response to persecution, a conflict often interpreted as an allegory of the contrasting political approaches associated with Martin Luther King Jr and Malcolm X. Despite some unwieldy scripts, Stewart and McKellen brought Shakespearean gravitas to their roles, making the ideological conflict between Xavier and Magneto genuinely compelling. The two would also reunite onstage in 2009 for a celebrated performance of Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot , a lifelong ambition for the pair. A Lifelong Commitment to Justice Off-screen, Stewart used his newfound fame to champion causes that mattered to him. He campaigned against domestic violence and championed women’s rights, trade unions, animal welfare, and greater recognition of PTSD among veterans. He also opposed Brexit and spoke out against right-wing demagogues, including Donald Trump. A resounding belief in fairness, ingrained in him from an early age, remained his guiding light. Stewart also revealed a gift for comedy, gleefully parodying his own dignified persona in appearances on Extras and the animated program Family Guy as well as a legendary turn hosting Saturday Night Live in 1994. Stewart continued to work right up until his death: his final film arriving in theaters this winter will see him reprise the part of Charles Xavier one last time. He will be remembered not just as one of the finest actors of his generation but also as a committed socialist who believed that compassion, equality, and solidarity were principles worth fighting for. For those of us who grew up watching Jean-Luc Picard, he offered something equally valuable: an example of leadership rooted not in intimidation or force but in intelligence, cooperation, and respect for others. It was a vision of humanity worth aspiring to, both on earth and among the stars. articles.title: Lula’s Historic Victory Repels Fascism and Opens a New Phase for Brazil
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By the CP of Brazil (CPdoB) October 26, 2026 Editorial by Portal Vermelho The people, with the youth at the forefront, led an epic triumph that opens a new chapter of social and democratic progress and the defense of national sovereignty. The reelection of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is, above all, a victory for the Brazilian people, with the youth playing a prominent role over the far-right forces that tried to stifle their hopes, curtail their rights, and subordinate the country to the greed of U.S. imperialism. It affirms a Brazil moving toward national development, with social inclusion, sovereignty, democratic freedoms, and rights for the people. This great achievement by the Brazilian people transcends the country’s borders. Amid the international rise of the far right, Lula’s victory is being celebrated by democratic, popular, and progressive forces from West to East. It is especially significant for the peoples and countries of Latin America and the Caribbean in the face of the United States’ neocolonial offensive in the region. Donald Trump’s neofascist government, which brazenly backed Flávio Bolsonaro, suffered a major defeat. The turnaround began with young people’s response to the adverse first-round result. The National Union of Students (UNE) drew up a nationwide mobilization calendar for the campaign Students with Lula: in the Streets and Online . The Socialist Youth Union (UJS) played a key role in bringing this agenda to fruition, alongside Free Homeland Youth (JPL). It was the spark that set off one of the largest popular mobilizations across the country since the return to democracy. The mobilization grew enormously as millions of ordinary people enthusiastically joined in, alongside the trade union federations, social movements as a whole, artists, and intellectuals. The digital battle was also decisive. Federal Deputy André Janones created the Lula’s Army channel on WhatsApp , which surpassed ten million followers and became a hub for distributing videos, audio messages, and mobilization guidance. Other influential voices joined in, and millions more, who had not previously been active online, entered the internet arena. The campaign faced illegal and criminal acts by Meta—the parent company of WhatsApp , Instagram , and Facebook —which restricted content about Lula and favored the far-right candidate. President Lula, at 80 years of age, was the great leader and decisive factor in this victory for the nation, the people, the youth, and the working class. This was due to a combination of qualities: his stature as a statesman; the trust he enjoys among the people; the political courage he once again showed in confronting fascism; his deep patriotism in rejecting Trump’s moves; his ability to unite broad forces; the drive to carry out a diverse and bold agenda across the country; and his ability to respond to the new demands of the class struggle, as he showed in the runoff by spreading messages on social media. And, concretely, when he realized that the vast majority of the ruling classes had aligned themselves with the far right, he broke through the encirclement by deepening his commitment to defending the rights of the Brazilian people, the country’s sovereignty, and democracy. This victory also reflects the role played by Vice President Geraldo Alckmin. He was tasked with broadening the dialogue beyond the forces already in Lula’s camp, mobilizing political leaders, mayors, businesspeople, religious representatives, and figures aligned with other political currents—from the center and center-right to the right. Together, the two fronts—the streets and social media—working in concert and coordinated with millions of activists and supporters, and grounded in the grassroots activism and leadership of progressive parties, confronted the power of the far-right alliance and much of the right, as well as the shameful bias of the powerful media monopolies. They exposed Flávio Bolsonaro and did what had seemed impossible: turned the election around and reelected President Lula. The Communist Party of Brazil (PCdoB), its activist base, and its leaders were on the front lines of this confrontation, which will shape the country’s present and immediate future. Lula’s fourth presidential term will have historic significance. It is born out of one of the greatest political confrontations in the history of the Republic. It emerges from the ballot box committed to an ambitious program: to kick-start sovereign development, including reindustrialization on new technological foundations that will create better jobs, with the wealth generated channeled into a new generation of rights for the people and greater recognition for work. It will deepen democracy and guarantee national sovereignty. To advance this agenda, Lula will need to build a broad alliance in support of his government and continue to draw strength from popular mobilization in the streets and online. The task will be even more challenging given the advance of the right and far right, reflected in the new composition of the National Congress and the election of governors from this political camp in key states. The victory thus opens a new phase of challenges, in which the strength secured at the ballot box must be turned into concrete advances for the country and the Brazilian people. A powerful far-right wave, propelled by Trump, had been surging forward, convinced it was unbeatable as it swept from the Caribbean to South America; the White House was already celebrating Brazil as its next conquest. But the Brazilian people, with the youth as the driving force, spoke out loud and clear: Not here! No one will fly a foreign flag in place of our green-and-yellow; no one will plunder our wealth; no one will take away our hard-won rights; no one will bury the democracy we fought so hard—and at the cost of so many lives—to win; we will not accept a return to the horrific, tragic past of fascism and the Bolsonaros; we will not accept anyone killing our plans and dreams of a better life! And so, in pursuit of a promising and thriving future for Brazil and its people, the heroic, epic journey of the runoff secured President Lula’s fourth term. After all, now is the time to celebrate this historic achievement by the Brazilian people! articles.title: “We Do Not Work for War”: Dockworkers in 113 Ports across Five Continents Join International Strike
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Nikos Mottas October 31, 2026 In Defense of Communism From the Mediterranean to the Indian Ocean, from Australia to the Americas, dockworkers and seafarers joined an unprecedented international day of coordinated industrial action on Friday, October 30, declaring that ports must serve the needs of the people rather than become logistical bases for imperialist wars.According to trade unions involved in the mobilization, workers in 113 ports across 22 countries and five continents participated in strikes, work stoppages, demonstrations and solidarity actions under the common slogan: “We do not work for war!” The international mobilization, supported by more than 25 trade unions, brought together workers from Greece, Italy, France, Spain, Turkey, Morocco, Germany, India and numerous other countries. Its central demands included an end to the transportation of weapons and military equipment through commercial ports, opposition to the militarization of port infrastructure, solidarity with the Palestinian people and the protection of workers’ lives, wages and working conditions. The action also demonstrated the growing determination of organized dockworkers to challenge the transformation of commercial shipping into an essential component of the machinery of war. The initiative followed months of international trade union coordination, including discussions among dockworkers’ organizations in Istanbul earlier this year. It also marked a significant expansion of previous mobilizations against arms shipments, particularly those destined for Israel. Italy: Mass demonstrations and a nationwide strike Italy witnessed some of the largest mobilizations of the day, as the grassroots trade union Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) called a 24-hour nationwide strike, linking opposition to war and military spending with demands for higher wages, stronger public services and relief from the rising cost of living. Demonstrations took place in at least 60 Italian cities. According to USB estimates, approximately one million people participated nationwide, although this figure has not been independently verified. In Genoa, dockworkers marched through the port before joining students and workers from other sectors in a massive demonstration. Protesters rejected the use of the city’s port as a military logistics hub, demanding that it remain a workplace serving the population rather than an operational base for imperialist interventions. In Naples, thousands of demonstrators marched through the waterfront area, singing the anti-fascist song Bella Ciao. Attempts by police to restrict access to the port failed to prevent protesters from surrounding the facilities. Large demonstrations were also reported in Rome, Milan, Bologna, Florence, Trieste, Bari, Padua and Reggio Calabria. Protesters repeatedly connected the enormous resources devoted to military expenditure with deteriorating public services, low wages and the difficulties facing working-class families. The participation of students and young people was particularly significant. Their mobilizations highlighted the contradiction between increasing military budgets and the chronic underfunding of education, housing and healthcare. France: Major ports brought to a standstill In France, the ports and docks federation of the General Confederation of Labour (CGT) organized a 24-hour strike that, according to union reports, achieved participation exceeding 90%. Operations were severely disrupted at several major commercial ports, including Le Havre, Dunkirk, Rouen and Nantes–Saint-Nazaire. At Le Havre, one of France’s principal maritime gateways, loading and unloading operations were halted. In Dunkirk, bulk cargo terminals were blocked, while at Nantes–Saint-Nazaire several vessels remained at their berths without being serviced. Workers at Marseille-Fos and other French ports also participated in the international mobilization, opposing the transportation of military cargo and the broader militarization of European maritime infrastructure. The French dockworkers linked their anti-war demands to the defense of wages, employment and social protections, rejecting government policies that prioritize military expenditure while imposing new burdens on working people. Greece: Piraeus becomes a major center of international solidarity In Greece, the country’s largest port, Piraeus, was brought to a standstill as dockworkers, seafarers, shipyard workers and employees from numerous other sectors participated in the strike. From the early morning, workers maintained strike pickets at the COSCO container terminals, while maritime unions organized stoppages aboard passenger vessels. Work also ceased in shipbuilding and repair facilities, including the industrial areas of Perama and Skaramangas. Approximately 3,000 dockworkers and seafarers participated in the walkout, according to Reuters, while thousands of demonstrators gathered in central Piraeus for a rally and march toward the port. The mobilization extended beyond maritime workers, with participation from metalworkers, teachers, healthcare employees, students, pensioners and other sections of the working population. During the rally, live connections with trade union representatives in Italy and France demonstrated the practical coordination taking place between workers in different countries. The demonstration concluded at the port, where protesters unfurled a gigantic banner declaring “WORKERS DO NOT WORK FOR WAR,” accompanied by red smoke flares and messages of solidarity addressed to dockworkers across the world. Strike actions also took place in Thessaloniki, where more than 200 containers and trucks were reportedly blocked during a three-hour stoppage, as well as in Patras and other Greek ports. The General Secretary of the Communist Party of Greece (KKE), Dimitris Koutsoumbas, attended the Piraeus mobilization, expressing solidarity with the striking workers and emphasizing the international character of their struggle. From Hamburg to Scandinavia: Solidarity against militarization In Germany, young dockworkers and apprentices at the Port of Hamburg organized a gathering and demonstration in support of the international strike. The action emphasized the importance of involving a new generation of workers in organized trade union activity and international solidarity. Support also came from healthcare workers and trade union organizations in other parts of Germany. In Sweden, the dockworkers’ union denounced the militarization of European ports and warned against the use of security legislation to restrict trade union rights. Danish trade unions likewise expressed solidarity, connecting rising military expenditure with cuts to social benefits, pressure on pensions, higher living costs and worsening economic conditions. Across these countries, the mobilization reflected a common concern: workers are increasingly being asked to bear the economic and human consequences of military policies over which they exercise little democratic control. Australia, India, Turkey and the Americas join the mobilization The international day of action began in Australia, where dockworkers mobilized in Melbourne from the early morning. Their demands included opposition to the handling of military cargo and solidarity with the Palestinian people. Workers at Port Botany, near Sydney, also expressed support for the international initiative, emphasizing that ports should serve the communities and workers who operate them. In India, dockworkers and seafarers participated in actions at Chennai and Mumbai, demanding peaceful ports and dignified employment. Indian maritime workers also highlighted the dangers faced by crews operating in regions affected by military conflicts. In Turkey, a 24-hour strike was called at ports including Haydarpaşa in Istanbul, where metalworkers joined dockworkers in demonstrations against military shipments. Mobilizations and solidarity initiatives also extended to Morocco, including the strategically important port of Tangier, while workers in Brazil’s port of Itajaí expressed their opposition to war and support for international solidarity. Trade union organizations in the United States and Mexico were also among those involved in the international coordination, with actions planned in the Americas as the mobilization moved across time zones. Workers confront the machinery of war The international strike took place amid escalating military conflicts and mounting dangers for maritime workers, particularly in the Middle East and the Black Sea. Trade unions have reported numerous attacks on commercial vessels, with seafarers killed, wounded or stranded in dangerous waters. Alongside their opposition to military shipments, workers demanded improved safety measures, higher wages and adequate medical protection aboard vessels operating near conflict zones. Campaign organizers estimated that the coordinated actions could affect approximately 52,000 containers and cargo worth $2.8 billion. Reuters noted that these figures could not be independently verified, while shipping analysts expected the overall disruption to international trade to remain limited because many stoppages lasted only one day. Nevertheless, the political significance of October 30 extended beyond the immediate economic impact. The coordinated action demonstrated the potential of international working-class organization across national borders, bringing together dockworkers, seafarers, industrial employees, students and other sections of the population around common demands. At a time when governments and powerful economic interests are expanding military expenditure and integrating transport infrastructure into war preparations, the striking workers asserted a different priority: ports, ships and the wealth produced through their labor should serve human needs, not destruction. From Piraeus to Genoa, from Marseille to Melbourne and from Hamburg to Gaza, the message of October 30 was unmistakable: the working class possesses both the collective strength and the international solidarity to challenge the machinery of war. articles.title: Brazilian Communist Parties React to Lula’s Electoral Victory and Bolsonaro’s Flight to the US
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Nikos Mottas October 30, 2026 In Defense of Communism EDITOR’S NOTE: Brazil has three Communist Parties. The PCdoB is part of the Lula governing coalition. The PCB and PCBR are not. Brazil’s communist parties have responded to the re-election of social-democrat Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and the subsequent flight of defeated far-right presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro to the United States, warning that the electoral defeat of Bolsonarism does not eliminate the threat of reactionary forces, coup attempts and imperialist interference.In separate statements, the Brazilian Communist Party (PCB) and the Brazilian Revolutionary Communist Party (PCBR) stressed the necessity of mass mobilization and independent working-class struggle, while offering distinct assessments of the post-election political situation. Lula’s victory in the October 25 presidential runoff followed an intense electoral confrontation with Bolsonaro, who had finished ahead in the first round. The outcome was followed by Bolsonaro’s departure for the United States, despite a Brazilian Supreme Court order requiring him to surrender his passports amid an ongoing investigation. In a statement issued on October 29, the PCB described Lula’s victory as a significant blow to the Brazilian far right and to the ambitions of US imperialism in Latin America. However, it warned that the conservative composition of Congress and the continuing influence of reactionary political forces meant that the struggle was far from over. The party expressed particular concern over Bolsonaro’s flight to the United States and his subsequent claims to be Brazil’s legitimately elected president. According to the PCB, the protection afforded to the defeated candidate by Donald Trump’s administration could become an instrument of political pressure against Brazil. Washington, it warned, might exploit allegations of political persecution to challenge the legitimacy of the election results, attack Brazilian institutions and encourage new destabilization campaigns. The PCB also raised concerns about the possible role of Argentine President Javier Milei’s government in facilitating Bolsonaro’s departure, pointing to the broader cooperation between Latin American far-right forces and US imperialism. Calling for the defense of the electoral result and national sovereignty, the party emphasized that resistance to neofascism must also confront neoliberalism, capitalist exploitation and the policies of class collaboration. A day earlier, on October 28, the Central Committee of the PCBR had issued its own assessment, placing particular emphasis on the decisive role of popular mobilization in Bolsonaro’s electoral defeat. According to the PCBR, the political turnaround between the two rounds was driven largely by spontaneous demonstrations involving workers, students and young people. These mobilizations, it argued, represented a rejection of Bolsonarism rather than an endorsement of Lula’s political programme. The revolutionary communists warned that the far right retained substantial political strength, including in Congress and state governments, and accused reactionary forces of attempting to obstruct voting and subsequently discredit the election results. The PCBR cautioned that these maneuvers could create conditions for another coup attempt and potentially provide a pretext for US intervention. At the same time, the party rejected any suggestion that Lula’s victory should lead workers to abandon their political independence. It characterized the Lula–Alckmin administration as a government of class collaboration, criticizing its fiscal austerity policies, concessions to capital and commitment to maintaining the existing bourgeois political order. Both parties had supported a vote for Lula against Bolsonaro in the second round, without abandoning their criticism of the social-democratic government or endorsing its political programme.
