articles.title: Venezuela: From Revolution to Recolonization
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Lucas Koerne r, Ricardo Vaz October 20, 2026 Internationalist 360 Between smiles and a handshake, Venezuelan Acting President Delcy Rodríguez thanked US President Donald Trump for “supporting the country’s return to multilateral forums,” following a face-to-face meeting on September 22 that she called “historic.” In her address before the UN General Assembly one day later, Rodríguez reiterated her gratitude to Trump while promising a “democratic transformation” of her country. The acting leader’s trip to New York, a mere nine months after the January 3 US bombings and kidnapping of President Nicolás Maduro and First Lady Cilia Flores, perfectly encapsulated the Venezuelan government’s international and domestic realignment with US imperialism in general and its MAGA faction in particular. In her speech , she euphemistically called the January 3 military strikes “the outcome of the exhaustion of domestic politics and heightened confrontation with the US,” basically holding Venezuela partially responsible for the imperialist attack it suffered. The abandonment of Maduro Rodríguez’s trip was as symbolic for what was said as for what was left unsaid. The acting leader and her entourage heaped praise on Trump and took turns posing for pictures. Rodríguez also maintained an undignified silence when Trump, addressing the UN, gloated about the January 3 military operation and abduction of Maduro, whom he called an “outlaw dictator,” while shamelessly boasting that “to the victor belong the spoils.” Maduro and Flores – currently detained in Brooklyn just 10 miles from UN headquarters and facing a show trial on ludicrous “narcoterrorism” charges – were not worth a single mention by Rodríguez. This stance has been backed by pro-government pundits who are increasingly dropping the “acting” label when referring to Rodríguez. Her government has effectively undermined Maduro and Flores’ sovereign immunity argument to get their charges dismissed. US Justice Department prosecutors told the court that Caracas, via its embassy in the US, had advocated to the State Department for Rodríguez to receive head-of-state immunity in an unrelated civil lawsuit in Florida. But, Venezuelan authorities have declined to do the same vis-à-vis Maduro and Flores in what the US Justice Department called “devastating silence.” The official indifference is even more remarkable given Flores’ documented health issues, heavily aggravated by the brutal kidnapping, which led defense attorneys to request that she be moved to house arrest during the trial. This silence contrasts with the Maduro government’s loud defense of Alex Saab, which repeatedly brought up his health issues under incarceration during the international campaign for his release. Saab is another prime example of the Rodríguez administration’s pragmatic rapprochement with Washington. He was irregularly handed over to US agencies in May and recently pleaded guilty in a US federal court in Miami, promising to cooperate against unnamed Venezuelan officials. An imperial satellite The Venezuelan leadership’s diplomatic activity in New York more broadly showcased a new foreign policy direction that is now unmistakably marching to Washington’s drum. Rodríguez held talks with International Monetary Fund and World Bank representatives, deepening reengagement with the Washington-based financial institutions that former President Hugo Chávez denounced as instruments of US imperialism and booted them out of the country. The specter of another IMF loan-and-adjustment package returns as the Rodríguez administration begins negotiations to restructure the country’s enormous and illegitimate debt. In addition, Rodríguez held sideline meetings with US allies only, such as Netherlands PM Rob Jetten, Trinidad and Tobago PM Kamla Persad-Bissessar and Chilean President José Antonio Kast. Rodríguez also hosted Paraguayan President Santiago Peña in Caracas before flying to the US. The right-wing Chilean and Paraguayan administrations had firmly backed US regime change efforts in Venezuela, leading the Maduro government to sever ties. Trinidad and Tobago’s case was even more egregious, with Caracas suspending all cooperation, including in key cross-border natural gas projects, after Port of Spain endorsed Washington’s military buildup and extrajudicial boat bombings on Venezuela’s doorstep in late 2025. Rodríguez and her team also broke with the Chavista tradition of holding meetings with global majority countries similarly under Washington’s gun, especially allies and strategic partners like Cuba, Iran, China and Russia. A customary event in Harlem, alongside Cuban officials and international solidarity movements, was scrapped as well. The acting president’s UN address exposed how anti-imperialism and the defense of multipolarity have vanished from the official discourse. Absent was the hitherto denunciation of Washington’s criminal wars across the globe, replaced by a vague expression of solidarity with “peoples who suffer war.” Nor was there any condemnation of US economic sanctions, which remain in place against Venezuela and its former allies. Rodríguez offered no words of support for Cuba as it faces a US blockade that gets more murderous by the day. There was no mention of Palestine either. Before January 3, Venezuelan representatives had never wasted an opportunity to reiterate support for the Palestinian cause and to expose the international community’s failure to rein in the genocidal, Western-sponsored settler colony. In contrast, Venezuela joined the US, Israel, Ukraine, Western European countries and Latin American right-wing governments in boycotting the UN’s commemoration of the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration. The 2001 World Conference Against Racism marked a milestone in the ongoing struggle to end racism and colonialism, provoking the ire of the US and Israel, which have led boycotts of every one of its commemorations. Fuel for a sputtering empire Along with the 180-degree foreign policy shift, the Rodríguez administration has moved to restructure the economy to the benefit of a declining US hegemon reeling from its strategic defeat in the war against Iran. With US officials’ input and supervision, Venezuelan authorities have overhauled energy and mining laws in the interest of multinational corporations, slashing taxes and royalties as well as ceding operational and commercial control. Corporate executives, often shepherded by Trump aides, have paraded through the presidential palace to sign agreements carving up Venezuela’s immense subsoil resources. A recent oil deal with the Trump administration, which Rodríguez also hailed as “historic,” will turn over 17 prime oilfields holding more than a fifth of Venezuela’s crude reserves to a private petroleum company, NABEP, controlled by the Pentagon. Furthermore, the US State Department will be able to buy 20 percent of NABEP’s output at cost, while having a right of first refusal for the remaining 80 percent, for which a Venezuelan oil official promised a major “sales discount.” In other words, Venezuela is going to supply energy below market price to the imperial war machine. Whatever revenue is ultimately left for Caracas is still going to be controlled by the US Treasury Department, under what Venezuelan state oil company (PDVSA) chief defended as a “state-to-state agreement.” A recent Financial Times report revealed that the White House is presently barring Venezuela from paying dividends to Russian and Chinese joint venture partners in a flagrant attempt to drive them out. Washington’s semi-colonial control extends beyond privileged access to natural resources, including strategic minerals. A looming privatization drive and debt restructuring process are likely to further entrench Venezuelan dependence on Western monopoly capital. At the same time, the US is also looking to turn the South American country into a captive market for its heavily subsidized agricultural output. Venezuela’s imports of staples such as rice and corn have skyrocketed this year, seriously threatening national production, especially small and mid-size campesino farms supplying much of the country’s food. (Ab)uses of history The speed and scope of Caracas’ realignment with Washington has made it an uphill battle for those still insisting that the acting Rodríguez government is merely conducting a “tactical retreat” without straying from the Bolivarian Revolution’s strategic horizon. One early line of argument was to invoke historical examples, such as the Brest-Litovsk treaty, to rationalize difficult concessions at gunpoint. However, the analogy grew ever more dubious with the passing months, as the Bolsheviks never renounced their anti-imperialist internationalism nor the nascent socialist state’s sovereignty over the commanding heights of the economy. The argument that subordinating the economy to US-led capital was akin to China’s post-1978 opening up belies the reality that Venezuela does not even manage its own export revenues and must have its expenses approved by the US State Department, subject to auditing by CIA-linked firms like Deloitte. Venezuelan government officials and unofficial spokespeople have also abused examples related to Chávez , namely his call for troops to stand down in the failed 1992 insurrection and the fact that he did not martyr himself in the 2002 coup that briefly overthrew his democratically-elected government. However, in both cases, Chávez never surrendered his core principles concerning independence and sovereignty. In 2002, he allowed himself to be taken prisoner by the putschists to avoid a bloodbath, but he did not resign and would not have sat quietly if Venezuela were turned into a US semi-colony overnight. On multiple occasions , Chávez underscored he was prepared to fight and die on the frontlines should Venezuela face an Iraq-style US invasion. There are other historical analogies that are, unfortunately, more appropriate. Iraq after the US invasion, like Venezuela, to this day does not control its oil revenues, which are deposited in a New York Federal Reserve account. Iraq was until recently under US military occupation, hosting some two dozen bases – a possibility that Trump has recently left open for Venezuela. In past months, the US has carried out extrajudicial executions on Venezuelan soil and deployed military assets in the wake of July’s double earthquake, including temporarily taking over operations at the Simón Bolívar International Airport and La Guaira port. Egypt under President Anwar Sadat is likewise a very instructive precedent. Sadat never renounced his predecessor Gamal Abdel Nasser, simply presenting his program as a “correction” of past mistakes. Yet he progressively dismantled the achievements of Nasserism, rolling back land reform and industrialization policies in favor of imperialist capital. Sadat also realigned Egypt from the Soviet Union to the US camp, going on to reestablish ties with Israel and abandon the Palestinian cause. Vietnam: The forgotten analogy Lacking justifications for the new alliance with the Trump administration, Venezuelan government officials and influencers have resorted to straw man arguments, claiming that the “international left” wanted the Venezuelan people to immolate themselves by confronting a vastly superior military foe. The official rhetoric eclipses what was until recently Caracas’ preferred historical analogy: Vietnam. In late 2025, as the US ramped up its military buildup, Venezuelan leaders warned that Trump would face a “second Vietnam” if he dared to attack. There were months of military drills and detailed preparations across the country, consistent with Venezuela’s asymmetric doctrine of “ prolonged people’s war ”. Ultimately it is impossible to know how much resistance Venezuela could have mounted against the US onslaught because the leadership opted not to fight. US air superiority and electronic warfare notwithstanding, Venezuelan defense officials have neglected to explain why only one of Venezuela’s 5,000 Russian-made Igla-S manpads – ideal for taking down low-flying helicopters and combat aircraft – was used. Venezuela’s armed forces offered no organized resistance on that fateful morning, leaving Maduro’s Cuban security detail virtually alone to confront the invader in what reportedly still proved a fiercely heroic firefight that left 32 Cubans dead. Though Venezuela might have been unable to avoid decapitation of its top leadership – either via capture or assassination – it could have raised the costs for the US empire to a politically unacceptable degree, potentially miring it in the sort of Iraq-style quagmire that the Trump administration most feared . Instead, almost overnight, the acting government seamlessly pivoted from vowing to combat imperialism by all means necessary to fawning over Trump and his underlings. Promises that not a “ single drop ” of Venezuelan oil would be shipped to the US in case of an attack were replaced by risible claims that supplying crude at cost to the Pentagon was Chávez’s plan all along. Unable to present a convincing case for the domestic and foreign policy U-turns, official and unofficial government spokespeople have also lashed out at criticism from the Latin American left. Most recently, former Colombian President Gustavo Petro slammed the Rodríguez administration for giving away the nation’s oil to Trump. Caracas responded with ad hominem invectives . At Washington’s behest, Venezuela has also halted all subsidized oil shipments to Cuba, which has added to the island’s gravest energy crisis in its history. Cuba’s Deputy Foreign Minister Carlos Fernández de Cossío recently said that Venezuela remained a “friendly” country, but added that “ally is too strong a word.” The cost of capitulation The human toll of resistance, whether in sanctions-besieged Venezuela or on the battlefields of West Asia, is always immense. However, as national liberation movements have long understood, the price of capitulation is inevitably higher, especially in the medium and long term. Chávez and Maduro clearly grasped this reality, rallying the masses to withstand decades of US hybrid warfare and forging close alliances with anti-imperialist states from Cuba to Iran. The cost of submission, meanwhile, is being borne by the Venezuelan laboring classes, from small farmers hard hit by US agricultural dumping to the urban semi-proletariat devastated by spiraling inflation resulting from Washington’s pilfering of the nation’s export earnings. For its part, Venezuela’s comprador bourgeoisie, in both its traditional and emergent fractions, stands to reap fabulous rewards from the demolition of the legislative pillars of the Bolivarian Revolution – viz., hydrocarbons, mining, housing and real estate, or forthcoming axing of labor and land laws – reasserting itself as a servile intermediary for US imperialism. There is no better example than NABEP owner Alejandro Betancourt, an oil mogul who amassed a fortune from often-unfulfilled state contracts dating back to 2009 and was hand-picked by the Trump administration as a middleman in the 25-year agreement backstopped by the Pentagon. The White House went as far as pressuring domestic and foreign courts to drop money laundering accusations against Betancourt. Rodríguez and her leadership faction likewise benefit from what analyst William Serafino has called the new regime of “co-government” with the Trump White House, tying their fortunes to the latter to outflank rivals and solidify the strategic alliance with local and imperialist capital. The current acting president is one of the architects of the post-2018 neoliberal economic package that was the fulcrum of a new governability pact with the local bourgeoisie, freezing wages and social spending in exchange for social “peace”. Indeed, as then vice president, Rodríguez reportedly brought Betancourt back to Venezuela in 2023, shuttering an investigation into his alleged corruption and key role in financing the self-proclaimed Juan Guaidó “interim presidency” during the first Trump administration. The episode is symptomatic of the Venezuelan government’s Faustian gambit to appease business sectors and maintain a modest economic recovery under crushing sanctions, but at the cost of slowly eroding its popular support base. The Maduro administration’s concessions hollowed out the Bolivarian Revolution’s sovereign edifice but its institutional foundations remained formally intact alongside the internationalist geopolitical scaffolding binding Venezuela to the broader Axis of Resistance. The post-January 3 semi-colonial offensive has set about demolishing this structure of political-military and economic independence. While the destruction can be repaired through sustained bottom-up mobilization advancing a national popular alternative to capitulation, it will likely be the outcome of a medium- and long-term process. Nevertheless, there are growing signs of revolutionary movements and intellectuals organizing to confront the US empire and its local agents and reconquer sovereignty as the cornerstone of any future socialist construction. What should be clear without a sliver of a doubt is that the “Rodrigato” – and the lumpen bourgeoisie it represents – has opted to pact with the Trump administration. Any revolutionary strategy to resist re-colonization must begin from concrete analysis of concrete conditions. Ignoring the acting Venezuelan leadership’s discourse and policies, pretending that there is a cunning secret plan being devised or trying to frame everything as a masterful 3D chess move, will ultimately hamper the most important task: fighting US imperialism. articles.title: The Democratic Party Still Hates the Left
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Margaret Kimberley, BAR Exec. Editor & Senior Columnist October 21, 2026 Black Agenda Report The Democratic Party is terrified of even small liberal reforms and will not abide left leaning democrats thwarting their plans for austerity and neoliberal orthodoxy. “I would rather the Republicans keep the House by five than the Democrats win by five, because if that happens, they’re hostage to the DSA. Hakeem cannot move. There’s no place for him to go.” – James Carville Polls indicate that democrats can win control of the House of Representatives in the November 3, 2026 mid-term elections. If accurate, left leaning democrats may win some of those seats and those victories would mean that voters are looking for progressive change. But James Carville, eminence grise of conservative democrats, wants to disempower them and their voters before any of them even get to Washington. So great is his antipathy that he would prefer a republican victory to giving the left any opportunity to give Democratic Party voters what they want. Carville had famously said of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) , “I wish they’d take the word Democrat out of their name. I have no idea why the democratic socialists — if you hate the Democratic Party so much, well, then don’t use our godd*mn. Go think of your own name.” The tantrum may have been silly but the intent was deadly serious. The Democratic Party will not permit any possibility of change, and even small reforms have been declared off limits. Just in case there was any confusion, Carville said so in public in a conversation with right winger Bill Kristol. James Carville was a strategist in Bill Clinton’s presidential campaign and was among those who developed “triangulation,” a fancy word describing the betrayal of everything that Democratic Party voters wanted. Clinton solidified the support of the Democratic Party’s “big tent” while he dismantled the right to seek public assistance that was first guaranteed by Franklin Roosevelt 60 years earlier. His “reforms” pushed millions of poor people further into poverty, as he also deregulated financial services which brought about the 2008 great recession and bank bailouts nearly 20 years after his first term as president. Clinton deregulated the media and the end result is that a handful of corporations control everything we read and watch. Everything from popular culture to the quality of news reporting has suffered ever since. His Crime Bill sent thousands of Black people to prison while he largely maintained the support of Black voters despite the damage done by him and the collaborationists among the Democratic Party Black misleaders. Carville’s finger prints are all over these policies which proved to be disastrous for millions of people. The welfare state has been under attack for decades as each inhabitant of the white house cuts more holes in the safety net. We were saved from Barack Obama’s “grand bargain” budget deal with republicans only because of that party’s intransigence. Political gridlock turned out to be our salvation. Congressional Black Caucus member Emmanuel Cleaver stood out from the crowd and rightly decried the move as a “sugar coated satan sandwich.” For good measure he added , “This debt deal is antithetical to everything the great religions of the world teach, which is take care of the poor, aged, vulnerable.” Donald Trump continued the tradition of building upon what his predecessors have done. Now that he has brought to life conservative fantasies in Proposition 2025, DOGE, and “starving the beast,” cutting government spending in ways that Clinton and Obama and Biden didn’t dare to do, we are told that bringing democrats back into control of congress is an absolute must. But Carville let the cat out of the bag so to speak. If even a few left leaning DSA democrats are elected to congress, the backroom deal making with republicans that is a constant in Washington may be endangered. While voters who are democrats are exhorted to vote blue no matter who, Carville and his ilk have let them know in no uncertain terms that they should at the very least temper their expectations. The donor class who decide who will or won’t be president are also quite clear. During his presidential campaign Joe Biden promised fat cat funders that he would not demonize them and that he needed them very badly. For good measure he also said, “Nothing will fundamentally change. No one’s standard of living will change.” Although he lied about that. The poor have since gotten poorer, and the rich have gotten richer, and Biden bears responsibility for that outcome. After he lost control of the House in the 2022 mid-term elections, he showed his willingness to go along with republican policies that cut Medicaid and SNAP benefits . Hakeem Jeffries, who may become Speaker of the House of Representatives, was part of that deal-making, signaling that Biden’s moves had his blessing. Of course Jeffries was vetted by the donor class and wouldn’t do otherwise. Now Carville says that Jeffries needs space to move, but on whose behalf? Lest anyone forget, Jeffries is neither principled nor very smart. Even a modicum of shrewdness would have kept him from holding a secret meeting with Jared Kushner , Trump’s son-in-law. We don’t know what they discussed, but one can assume that Kushner’s agenda included a request not to investigate Trump or his family or to call for impeachment. Jeffries has already backtracked on his longstanding support of Medicare for All, a much-needed program that has the backing of most democrats. What good does it do Democratic Party voters, particularly Black voters, to so eagerly desire what has proven to be illusory again and again? If nothing else, we should be grateful to James Carville for reminding us all of the reality of politics in the U.S. The billionaire class calls the shots. Even with a democratic president like Joe Biden, they may pretend that they will provide a Build Back Better bill with some reforms and assistance to working people, but ultimately they will backtrack because that is not what the oligarchs want. Carville is the public face of the oligarchy. He knows they will not allow any liberal reforms. He wants Jeffries or whoever is Speaker of the House to have that space to do deals and engage in pretense. We should all know that pretense when we see it and remember that the Democratic Party donor class and its errand boys and errand girls hate the left, are pledged to defeat them, and will never give them any quarter. -Margaret Kimberley is the author of Prejudential: Black America and the Presidents . articles.title: New Biography of Elizabeth Gurley Flynn
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Mary Anne Trasciatti, Rosemary Feurer October 10, 2026 In Elizabeth Gurley Flynn: The Rebel Girl, Democracy, and Revolution (Rutgers University Press, 2025), historian Mary Anne Trasciatti traces Elizabeth Gurley Flynn’s path to becoming one of the most important labor radicals in US history, taking part in almost every major left campaign of the first half of the twentieth century. Often seen in biography and popular memory as a relic of the IWW, the Flynn of Trasciatti’s new book instead takes form as a dynamic and profoundly talented organizer who consistently devoted her life to building an American left tradition committed to free speech, democracy, and working-class power. A strong advocate for racial and gender equality, her skill and commitment to these principles made her a critical figure on the left across many decades of campaigns and organizational commitments. Rosemary Feurer interviewed Trasciatti about her new biography. First, could you start by telling us what we should know about Elizabeth Gurley Flynn, why she’s an important figure in labor history. Elizabeth Gurley Flynn spent half a century as an activist for working people in the United States. and yet she’s barely known now unless you’re into radical or labor history. Even then, people know mostly her early years as the Rebel Girl of the Industrial Workers of the World. In her lifetime she was a household name among working-class people, practically a celebrity, and she knew everybody.She was born in New Hampshire in 1890 and grew up in New York hearing about the Irish independence struggle and seeing working-class people struggle all around her. She was precocious, a socialist as a teenager, and then a Wobbly, a member of the Industrial Workers of the World, which was a radical union dedicated to organizing all workers in all industries. The Wobblies had no truck with electoral politics. They believed that change would come on the shop floor: workers would take over the means of production and ensure that workplace democracy was extended into society generally. And she was very popular as an organizer and an agitator—a “jawsmith,” as the IWW called it—because she was super smart and super well-spoken. So, she traveled around organizing workers into unions, standing up for workers who were on strike, and defending free speech.The first couple of chapters of the book are about the free speech fights in Missoula and Spokane to show how important Flynn was to them and how important they were for organizing workers. In the early twentieth century, cities like Missoula and Spokane passed laws against street speaking to keep the IWW from organizing “undesirables,” and Flynn devised many of the tactics the union used to defy these laws. The rationale was, “If we can’t speak on the street corners to organize workers, we’ll violate the law and speak anyway, get arrested, and fill the jails until the laws are changed.” When she led the free speech fights, Flynn was young, beautiful, and pregnant, and the call for Wobblies to “defend” her helped launch the tradition of recruiting hobos into those fights. Flynn was involved in just about every cause the left took up between 1906, when she first became an activist, until her death in 1964: free speech; labor defense; union organizing; strikes; antifascism; campaigns against deportations, lynching, the poll tax, and housing discrimination; you name it. In no time, Flynn earned a reputation as an important and popular organizer. Wherever she went, she attracted crowds and media attention. Young women were enamored of her. She inspired them to organize and to be on the front lines, for instance, during strikes in the textile mills in Lawrence, Massachusetts in 1912 and the silk mills in Paterson, New Jersey in 1913-1914. During World War I, Flynn was arrested in the federal raids on the IWW. She escaped trial by pleading with President Woodrow Wilson in a letter, essentially saying, “I’m a mom, how can I be a radical?” (It’s a little cringy.) It was at this time that she broke from the Wobblies. But she didn’t abandon the movement. In 1918, she founded the Workers Defense Union to defend anyone – trade unionist, socialist, anarchist, Wobbly, and later, communist – prosecuted under the Espionage Act, which made it a crime to hinder the war effort in any way. The left is really good at fighting amongst itself, but Flynn bucked that trend and brought people together around a shared goal: to defend free speech for labor activists. In the early 1920s, she became an antifascist. We tend to think of anti-fascism in the United States as beginning with the rise of the Nazis and opposition to the Nazis. But really, it was Italian radicals in the 1920s who saw their friends, relatives, and comrades brutally repressed by Mussolini’s regime and organized in opposition. Flynn was in a romantic relationship with Italian anarchist Carlo Tresca at that time, and what she learned convinced her that fascism was an anti-democratic ideology that threatened not just Italy, but all people around the globe. She saw the Ku Klux Klan and the American Legion as particularly American forms of fascism, rooted in racism but also attempting to squash working-class organizing. After a personal crisis in 1926, Flynn left public life and spent the better part of ten years living with anarchist Marie Equi in Washington State. The Popular Front brought her back to New York and to politics. That was the moment when the Communist Party turned from advocating the overthrow of capitalism by revolution to supporting Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal and building alliances with liberals in the struggle against fascism. The Popular Front was very appealing to Flynn. She joined the Communist Party of the United States in 1937 and remained a Communist for the rest of her life. So, you could say that Flynn was a lifelong American radical: first, a socialist, then, a syndicalist, and finally, a Communist. She spoke at Northern Illinois University around 1961. There’s a transcript of it at NIU’s library. And all of those students were just interested in her Wobbly past. Some other biographers have followed that. Your book insists that there is a throughline with the earlier periods of her life, not a significant contrast. So can you talk about that a little bit? What was your choice there in thinking about how to make sense of her life? Elizabeth Gurley Flynn was so cool and such a fierce champion for the working class, and it bums me out that she is not better known, especially among young people. I wanted to do something to help change that. Flynn was involved in just about every cause the left took up between 1906, when she first became an activist, until her death in 1964: free speech; labor defense; union organizing; strikes; antifascism; campaigns against deportations, lynching, the poll tax, and housing discrimination; you name it, I could keep going. I asked myself, “How can I tell the story of this incredible organizer and activist in a way that hangs together and doesn’t repeat what had already been said about her a million times?” I realized there was something I could trace from the beginning of her career to the end, and that was her defense of the First Amendment and her commitment to free speech and civil liberties. At the time she was doing this work, not everyone thought it was necessary. Accounts of the Wobbly free speech fights note that there was controversy over them: there were people who thought they were taking away from the important work of organizing. Flynn was part of an earlier radical tradition that saw the anti-capitalist left as part of the revolutionary tradition the nation was founded upon. And I’ve heard historians say the same within the last ten years. What is your view? Flynn—and I agree with her—rejected that assessment, because without the right to free speech and assembly in public space, you can’t organize. During the Paterson silk strike in 1913, for example, local government and law enforcement tried to shut down access to halls, streets, and parks. What do you do if you have thousands of workers on strike and no place to hold a meeting? How do you keep up morale? Build solidarity? Discuss strategy? You could use private homes, which they did. For example, the Botto House in Haledon, New Jersey, the town next to Paterson, where they had a socialist mayor. But a labor union can’t rely on access to people’s homes during a strike. Flynn understood free speech not as an abstract right. She knew that speech is a concrete action. It’s the way you reach people, the way you organize, the way you bring the message to the workers, because you can’t rely on the workers coming to you. They’re tired. They don’t have access – they don’t know you’re there if you’re in some far-off place. For her, freedom of speech, freedom of assembly, freedom of the press were essential tools, the necessary preconditions, for organizing workers. You can’t organize people if you can’t reach them. Flynn never wavered in her commitment to civil liberties. She fought for workers’ right to the streets, to organize a strike even during wartime, to a fair trial even if you’re an immigrant with radical ideas; or to be a member of whatever political organization or party you choose, even if that party is the Communist Party. And we should mention that the Communist Party was legal when these prosecutions mostly were taking place. Exactly. And for me, that’s how the book hangs together. It doesn’t matter whether Flynn is a socialist or a Wobbly or a Communist. She’s an organizer of working-class people, a radical organizer with a profound commitment to civil liberties. That’s a little ironic for some people, but she was utterly devoted to defending the First Amendment. When I started writing this book, we were in a moment—I think we’re moving away from it—where to be an activist on the left was to really focus on the flaws of the United States. But Flynn was part of an earlier radical tradition that saw the anti-capitalist left as part of the revolutionary tradition the nation was founded upon. To give one example, the Declaration of Independence was an important tool for the Wobbly free speech fights. Wobbly orators would stand on a streetcorner soapbox, read from the declaration, because a lot of these people were not eloquent speakers, and wait to be arrested so they could demand their First Amendment rights. It blows a lot of people’s minds to think about a left that says “This revolutionary tradition is ours, and the people who are grinding us under their heels are the ones violating its promise. We need to wrench the American revolutionary tradition away from an imperialist, capitalist, racist society and hold it to its true roots, which are freedom from tyranny, freedom from oppression, freedom for all.” For her, freedom of speech, freedom of assembly, freedom of the press were essential tools, the necessary preconditions, for organizing workers. You can’t organize people if you can’t reach them. During the Wobbly free speech fights there was a conversation about free speech and civil liberties that reverberated around the country and as far away as Australia. This kind of conversation is called popular constitutionalism, and it goes something like this: “You don’t need people trained at law schools to tell you what the First Amendment says. You can decide for yourself. You read the Constitution, you read the First Amendment, and there it is.” People really responded to that idea, even if they didn’t know what it was called. They were empowered by it. They debated in multiple languages, in their own newspapers, in public forums. This conversation was important, and Flynn helped set it in motion. And I think that’s key. It exemplifies Jim Barrett’s “Americanization from the bottom up” thesis: in their debates about the Wobbly free speech fights, working-class people figured out what this country means for themselves. I think that’s a remarkable achievement, and it deserves to be more widely known and celebrated, because it provides inspiration in this present moment of “America 250.” Who do we include in the story? Why does this American revolutionary tradition matter? Well, Flynn would say it matters because working-class people can exploit that tradition, in the best sense of the word, and make it their own and say: freedom and liberty and the good things in life—we deserve all that. Your book suggests that the Irish networks she travelled in contributed to this perspective. Her identity as an Irish American was very important to Flynn. She felt that if you were true to your Irish roots, you had to be a socialist; you had to be an advocate for the underdog; you had to do labor defense. She saw Irishness as a responsibility: if you are Irish, you are part of a history of exploitation, particularly of working people—of rigged juries and stolen wages and oppression of all kinds—and you have an obligation to stand up for the oppressed and the exploited wherever you find them. She was really frustrated by Irish American police. She called them “fat-jowled Hibernians” and a few other things. Flynn was deeply committed to Irish socialist James Connolly’s idea of a workers’ republic. She helped found the Irish Socialist Federation with Connolly when she was just a teenager. She was also friends with Jim Larkin. She learned from him as well. There’s a moment after the Paterson silk strike when Flynn is forbidden from speaking in that city. A group of affluent women in New York decked her out in fancy clothes so that she could sneak into a meeting hall and address workers. That was 1915. I think she got the idea to disguise herself from Larkin, who during the 1913 Dublin Lockout wore a disguise so he could make his way past police in the crowd before taking it off to address workers from a balcony. Unlike Larkin, Flynn didn’t fool anyone with her disguise, but it was a good idea. Flynn was also an anti-imperialist and anti-colonialist, because she believed that to be Irish was to carry with you the history of colonialism and imperialism and all the exploitation they entailed. She supported the Mexican Revolution and the Indian independence movement. In the offices of the Workers Defense Union, she had Indian anti-colonial pamphlets printed. She encouraged Indians and Irish to march together in the St. Patrick’s Day parade in New York. She was committed not just to the creation of a workers’ republic in the United States, but also to supporting anti-colonial struggles around the globe, because she was Irish. In 1952, when Flynn was called to testify before the Subversive Activities Control Board, which was established by the McCarran Act to identify and investigate subversive organizations, she was asked if she owed allegiance to any foreign power. And she said, “No foreign power at all. But I admit I have a soft spot for Ireland.” And she meant that. What they wanted to suggest was that her only loyalty was to the Soviet Union. Exactly. She was loyal to the United States, but she had a soft spot for Ireland. And when she was convicted under the Smith Act and sent to prison, the Irish responded. There were calls for her release. There were celebrations of her as a socialist and advocate of the workers’ republic. So, the warmth went both ways. She was appreciated in Ireland. She saw Irishness as a responsibility: if you are Irish, you are part of a history of exploitation, particularly of working people—of rigged juries and stolen wages and oppression of all kinds—and you have an obligation to stand up for the oppressed and the exploited wherever you find them . Another fascinating part of your book is the story of how Flynn was part of the rise of civil liberties, but then was expelled from the ACLU? Flynn founded the Workers Defense Union in 1918, initially as part of the Liberty Defense Union, which was the precursor to the ACLU. She later described the WDU as “a godchild of the ACLU”. And there was a lot of complementary work going on there. Flynn helped organize the ACLU, but the other organizers really didn’t know how to reach working-class people, immigrants, people whose languages and cultures were unfamiliar to them. They turned to Flynn and said, “help us; be our liaison with working-class people and movements.” These people were good-hearted and well-heeled, part of an American elite. Flynn always preferred hanging out with working-class people, but she could talk to elites; she could code-switch, in contemporary language. At the same time, she was beloved by immigrants of various ethnic and national groups. Her speeches were published in Finnish newspapers, in Italian newspapers. These communities knew her. So, she could be the liaison between the American liberal elite and working-class communities, many of them immigrant communities. The Workers Defense Union worked on behalf of Emma Goldman, Eugene Debs, Sacco and Vanzetti, and many more individuals with little or no name recognition. The reputation that Flynn for this work got her elected to the executive committee of the ACLU in the 1930s. But after the 1939 Nazi-Soviet Pact there’s a growing rift in the ACLU between New Deal liberals and anti-communists. One reason for the rift is that the ACLU was moving in a new direction on civil liberties. The organization was founded in 1920, largely, though not only, to assist labor activists who were imprisoned or otherwise targeted for their activism. But after the Nazi-Soviet Pact, it pivoted to embrace a value-neutral position on civil liberties, treating free speech as the sign of a democratic society. And for Flynn, that didn’t fly. She believed civil liberties are a starting point for democracy, a necessary precondition for balancing power between “haves” and “have nots.” The rift continued to grow. In 1940, the ACLU passed a resolution, not unlike what was recently debated in Congress, that fascism and communism are equally bad because both are authoritarian ideologies, and anybody who was a member of a fascist organization or a communist organization had no place on the board of the ACLU. A lot of people called it a “Communazi” resolution. Flynn was the most obvious target for that resolution, and she saw it that way. It became personal, and it got ugly. And while, yes, there was disagreement over the ACLU’s move towards a value-neutral approach to free speech, the resolution was a reflection of a rising tide of anti-communism. Members of the board were afraid of being red-baited. They were worried about J. Edgar Hoover, worried about being called before the House Un-American Activities Committee and losing political and financial support. Because they couldn’t get Flynn to resign from the board, they put her on trial. She spoke in her own defense quite eloquently. She called out board members for their red-baiting and noted that if she had been targeted during the ACLU’s early years, the ACLU would have endorsed her cause. Her argument was, “You’re saying I violated my commitment to free speech by becoming a Communist. One, you knew I was a Communist when you elected me to the board the first time and when you renewed my term. And two, you are the ones who have violated your commitment to the First Amendment with this political litmus test.” Alas, she lost. The vote was tied, and the tie was broken, I think, by John Haynes Holmes, who voted to have Flynn expelled from the board. The decision was very controversial when it was brought to a nationwide vote. Some members resigned from the organization in protest. Others worried that the ACLU was violating its own principles and setting a dangerous precedent. But several members around the U.S. cheered the move. What else is noteworthy about these speeches is how she tied the experience of Irish Americans to that of African Americans. Flynn’s experienced her expulsion from the ACLU as a personal betrayal, and I think she was right. But she also realized that when the going got tough, her former civil liberties allies would not stand up to red-baiting for anyone. And I think this is important. When the ACLU expelled Flynn, they basically gave the liberal left’s seal of approval to red-baiting and anti-communism. We know, for example, that organizations passed their own “Communazi” resolutions that were modeled on the ACLU one. The liberals turned toward what they called “principled anti-communism,” and this important organization was authorizing that perspective. A lot of resolutions were passed in labor councils in the aftermath of this. Yes, and what you couldn’t say to these labor councils or other organizations was, “oh my gosh, this is in violation of everything you stand for!” Because they would point to the ACLU and say, “if the organization dedicated to defending free speech can find a principled stand on anti-communism, so can we.” The ACLU was divided at this time, too, right before they tossed her out, about the sit-down strikes. They waffled in their position on the sit-down strikes at General Motors. With this more neutral position: they make free speech and property rights both somewhat sacrosanct. Yes, because the sit-downers were arguing, “We have a right to our jobs. We’re not claiming a right to the actual property of the factory, but we’re sitting down on our right to our jobs.” And the ACLU really waffled on that. And they also waffled in their response to Ford’s attack on UAW organizers at the River Rouge plant. The thinking was, “Well, employers don’t have a right to beat up organizers, but they do have a right to discourage unionization.” The ACLU was now defending union busting in the interest of a value-neutral approach to free speech! And Flynn was like, are you kidding me? Her position—and I think you see something very similar in the preamble to the National Labor Relations Act—was that working people need collective organizing because they are not on a level plane with employers. If we want to avoid disrupting society completely, we have to level the playing field, and collective organizing and collective bargaining are the way to do that. Unless you have free speech, you don’t have that level playing field. So, to say that Ford has the same rights as the UAW organizers and that union busting is okay—well, Ford has so much more power, and you’re not recognizing power. That frustrated her. When the ACLU expelled Flynn, they basically gave the liberal left’s seal of approval to red-baiting and anti-communism. And there’s the idea that there are such things as collective free speech rights. With that change of course toward individual free speech, we lose a lot of that, and the ideas behind it are still resonant. Like you said, we’re celebrating America 250, and our history department has a series starting in November on figures in American history. I tried to put Elizabeth Gurley Flynn into the mix there, and was turned down. I’m shocked. No, I’m not. When I read your book, it’s this amazing figure who sees her positions as consistent, at least on those issues of defense and the way labor should organize, and on the revolution’s legacy and all of that. But I guess it’s still a hard sell, even after the Cold War is over. But maybe, bringing it up the way you do, it’s not as hard to sell her as a heroic figure as it may have been during the Cold War? When Flynn was imprisoned at Alderson after her Smith Act trial, she was asked to write an article for the Fourth of July issue of the prison newspaper, the Alderson Eagle. In her article she links the revolution to FDR’s Four Freedoms. It’s a really interesting move. They also asked her and Claudia Jones, a Trinidad-born member of the Communist Party and dear friend, to help desegregate the prison when the order came to desegregate, because they knew that as Communists, they were committed to racial justice and racial equality. Even in prison people grudgingly acknowledged this stuff. Yes. There is this proud part of the tradition in the Communist Party, and it links to her earlier life too: the ideas of freedom of speech, freedom of assembly, and anti-fascism. Tell us a little more about that. Gurley Flynn was always organizing across boundaries of race and gender. Although she wasn’t a feminist, she thought it essential to organize women. And she also thought it essential to organize Black workers in the United States: Caribbean Americans, African Americans, Black workers of all kinds. During the first Red Scare, when the Messenger , the newspaper published by socialists A. Philip Randolph and Chandler Owen, was suppressed because of its antiwar position—Black Americans were among the first to see the acute irony of the nation fighting to make the world safe for democracy while many of its citizens were denied democracy based on their skin color, and they were very straightforward about that—there was a meeting in Harlem, and Flynn was one of the speakers. She was billed as a “Most Gripping and Scholarly Irish Woman Orator” – I love that! And after the Elaine Massacre, when organizing among sharecroppers in Elaine, Arkansas, was brutally repressed, she spoke again in Harlem. Those speeches were transcribed, because New York had passed an anti-radical law that meant state agents would be going to the meetings and transcribing them. She used to mock those agents mercilessly. And thank goodness for them, in a way; it’s a bittersweet thing, because now we have these transcripts. When you read them, you get a real sense of how brilliant she was as a fundraiser. She would speak last, because she was one of the main events, and then the hat would be passed and she’d be up at the microphone saying: “Oh, I hear a lot of jingling, but we need some paper. So, let’s hear it for the paper. And how about the Irish? You need to step up here, because I know a lot of you, and you don’t want me to see you on the street and know that you didn’t put anything in the basket.” She just harangued the heck out of people in the audience, and they ponied up money. She played an important role as the public face of the CPUSA, connecting the Party to the history of labor organizing in the United States, and she was very popular among rank-and-file members of the Party. But what else is noteworthy about these speeches is how she tied the experience of Irish Americans to that of African Americans. “My people came here because they were fleeing starvation and persecution; your people were forced to come here. But we both came here and were met with exploitation, and so ours is a common struggle and we must work together.” She would tell Black workers in the audience, “You can’t fight alone. You need to join the IWW. This is the organization that organizes across racial boundaries. You need to fight for your rights; fight with the IWW.” Later, in the 1920s, she advocated organizing among Black people, by Black people. But during the first Red Scare, she called for multiracial alliances. And she would say to the white workers, Irish American and otherwise. “You need to stop this nonsense. We are all exploited, oppressed people, and it is our responsibility as Irish people to extend a hand across the racial barrier. We will never succeed in the struggle if we don’t tear down the racial barrier. “ And people responded. In the transcription you see that she got cheers from the audience. Her message was simple. I think it fell on fertile soil. People really responded. Flynn carried that message forward into the 1920s and into the 1930s in her work with the CPUSA. So it wasn’t that she became an anti-fascist and an anti-racist because of the CP. She brought work she had already been doing into the Party: against lynching, against housing discrimination, against job discrimination, articulating the triple jeopardy status of Black women. Her relationship with Claudia Jones and other Black communists is not to be underestimated. There was mutual respect and mutual fondness. Angela Davis says that Flynn was one of the few white women at the time who understood the plight of working-class Black women. I think that’s remarkable, and it’s a real model as we grapple with race and class. She offers inspiration for how to organize across those barriers. Your book doesn’t flinch when discussing the difficulties she had in the Communist Party. Her first act as a Communist, in 1937, was to speak at a fundraiser for the Abraham Lincoln Brigade, the volunteer brigade from the United States that joined the International Brigades to fight against Francisco Franco’s fascists in Spain. As a longtime anti-fascist, this was a perfect way to begin her association with the CPUSA. The Party’s commitment to building the CIO also appealed to the labor organizer in Flynn. She played an important role as the public face of the CPUSA, connecting the Party to the history of labor organizing in the United States, and she was very popular among rank-and-file members of the Party. Sadly, Party leaders didn’t respect Flynn as they should have. She was a woman and they kept shunting her into “women’s work.” (The CP was much better at dealing with issues of race than it was at dealing with issues of gender.) Also, she wasn’t a theorist. She was a Marxist, I suppose, but she didn’t go around quoting Marx. What she did was talk to working-class people and she was very good at it. She got a lot more, intellectually and emotionally, out of talking to coal miners in northeastern Pennsylvania, than sitting around with Party leaders theorizing about this or that approach to revolution. So, she was considered kind of an intellectual lightweight, which I think is a real irony: a party that aims to organize the working class to overthrow capitalism finds that the member who probably has the best rapport with working-class people, and the most love for them as a class and as individuals, is an intellectual lightweight. But there you have it. She was really important to the CP when the Nazi-Soviet Pact was announced. I’m sure she was devastated by the pact, because here’s an anti-fascist to the bone since the early 1920s who is now part of an organization attempting to make peace with the Nazi-Soviet Pact, the agreement between the Soviet Union and Germany that neither would attack the other. That was hard. And that was the moment when support for the Popular Front really began to crumble. Roger Baldwin was gobsmacked by it, and he wasn’t alone. So, we begin to see support peeling away on the liberal left, which begins to question the Party, its members, and its leaders in particular, for suddenly being able to defend the Nazi-Soviet Pact. Flynn remained an anti-fascist throughout this period, but she was a good Communist, so she didn’t criticize the pact. The party line was that the war going on in Europe was an imperialist war, a war of imperial powers, not an anti-fascist struggle anymore. Of course, that all changes when Germany invades the Soviet Union, and suddenly we’re back to the being a war against fascism, and Flynn falls in line again. Before the Soviet Union and the United States were allied in the war, the head of the CPUSA, Earl Browder, was arrested, and Flynn led the campaign for his defense, continuing the work she had been doing since she was a Wobbly. She co-chaired the defense campaign with Tom Mooney, who was actually very sick and in intensive care, on oxygen. But he had an important symbolic function. Like Flynn, he was an Irish American radical, and a link between the Party and the history of labor activism and organizing in the US. He did not live to see Browder released. The Smith Act, a.k.a., the Alien Registration Act, which was passed in 1940, made it a crime to advocate the overthrow of the U.S. government by force and violence. The first group prosecuted under the Smith Act were Trotskyists, and when that happened, the CP, including Flynn, did not come to their defense. Donna Haverty-Stacke’s book Trotskyists on Trial is great for anybody who’s interested in this story. The case of the Trotskyists should have served as a warning to the CP, but of course it didn’t. A few years later, in 1948, the party’s leadership was rounded up, arrested, and prosecuted under the Smith Act. These were the “first-string” Smith Act defendants in New York. Flynn was not among them, and she was kind of miffed that she wasn’t, because— She thought she should be first string. Yeah: “I’m a somebody, and I wasn’t rounded up.” She did for her comrades what she had done for Earl Browder and for the Wobblies and Sacco and Vanzetti, and many others: she formed a defense campaign and advocated for their release. It was kind of a hard sell by this time. In past defense campaigns she had organized the goal was to bring people together and say, “whatever your ideological differences, this is a threat to free speech and civil liberties generally in the United States, and it is a way to hobble organizing among working-class people, and we need to put a stop to it.” But it was a hard sell for the Smith Act defendants, and the campaign became a Communist endeavor. In 1951, Flynn herself was arrested as part of the “second-string” Smith Act indictments. She chose to defend herself in court, and to lead a defense campaign for herself and the other Communists who were arrested with her. And like the first Smith Act defendants, she and other Second String defendants were found guilty and sent to prison. Flynn served about two and a half years at the federal women’s prison in Alderson, along with Claudia Jones. While she was in prison, there was division in the Party over the revelations about Stalin that followed his death and the Soviet invasion of Hungary. Flynn tried not to take a stand; she felt that she needed to consult with comrades before she decided which side to support. When she was released from prison, she initially saw some value in the proposed reforms, which would have oriented the Party away from an internationalist outlook toward a more American outlook, one that put conditions in the United States at the forefront of organizing. But for reasons I don’t quite understand, in the end she decided she didn’t support those changes. Flynn wrote the first half of her autobiography before she went to Alderson and it was published while she was in prison. She never got around to writing the second half, because she was constantly drawn into defense work, mostly defending the Party and its members from prosecution under the McCarran Act. She complained about not having time to write and it’s a shame because it would be interesting to read her thoughts about her life as Communist. Under the terms of the McCarran Act, members of the Communist Party could not apply for or hold a passport. Flynn, who had traveled to Europe and the Soviet Union after World War II, had her passport confiscated, as did another Party member, Herbert Aptheker. They appealed the decision, and while their case was making its way to the Supreme Court, she wrote and spoke in defense of the right to travel as a civil liberties matter. Her argument was interesting. She criticized the use of a litmus test for citizens who wished to travel and pointed out that when federal authorities confiscated her passport, they were censoring her politics and denying those beyond the borders of the US the right to hear her point of view. She continued to speak against the McCarran Act and for civil liberties even after the court had her passport reinstated. But her audiences were smaller and smaller, and older and older. She had joined the party in the 1930s, when, if you wanted to be at the forefront of working-class organizing and making change in the United States, you were likely either to flirt with joining the CP or to join outright. By the time of the passport denials, Flynn and other Party leaders were speaking on college campuses, but the energy just wasn’t there anymore. The torch had passed to a new generation of organizers. When her passport was granted again and she was able to travel, she went to the Soviet Union. She had every intention of going to Ireland. But she never made it. She got sick and died in Moscow in 1964. There was a big state funeral for her there. Her ashes were then brought back to the United States, and were buried in Chicago, in the same cemetery as the Haymarket martyrs and Emma Goldman. There’s a lovely marker there with a great epitaph: The Rebel Girl. Fighter for Working Class Emancipation. -M ary Anne Trasciatti is the daughter and granddaughter of garment workers and coal miners. She is Director of Labor Studies at Hofstra University and president of Remember the Triangle Fire Coalition. She is the co-editor of Talking to the Girls: Intimate and Political Essays on the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire (2022) as well as Where Are the Workers?: Labor’s Stories at Museums and Historical Sites (2022). -Rosemary Feurer is Professor of History at Northern Illinois University. She is the author of Radical Unionism in the Midwest, 1900-1950, among other books and essays. She is working on The Illinois Mine Wars, 1860-1940 and a new biography of Mary Harris “Mother” Jones. -This interview first appeared in Labor Online , a newsletter of LAWCHA, the Labor and Working Class History Association. articles.title: Demonstrations throughout Colombia Target New President and US Intervention
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By W.T. Whitney Jr. October 21, 2026 The anti-government demonstrations that recently rocked Colombia erupted only two months after President Abelardo de la Espriella took office, on August 7. The framework surrounding them is large. Colombian academician Manuel Humberto Restrepo Domínguez refers to a “humanistic outburst against fascism and capitalism in its genocidal phase … circulating through the streets of major cities in Europe, Latin America, and — starting on October 14 — in Colombia.” On that day, Colombians pilloried both the new president and US pretensions. Demonstrations took place in 62 locations and the capital cities of all 31 departments. Marshalled against the far-right De la Espriella, a novice politician, were thousands of protesting and marching unionists, workers, students, teachers, feminists, indigenous people, past office holders, and veteran activists of all stripes. The outpouring of dissent was extraordinary. De la Espriella had succeeded Gustavo Petro, president of Colombia’s only progressive government, ever. Petro accompanied marchers in Bogota, as did Senator Iván Cepeda, the defeated presidential candidate of the Historic Pact Party, founded by Petro. The margin by which Cepeda lost was less than one percent. A US-facilitated social-media storm contributed to his defeat. On the day prior to October 14, De la Espriella fired up opposition forces by issuing his repressive Decree 1525. The measure stipulates that dialogue with protesters not “condition, suspend, or postpone enforcement actions directed individually against those who commit acts of violence.” In general, presidential decrees and slogans are setting the new government’s course, not legislation. Nelson Lombana Silva, blogger and Communist Party activist, characterizes the protests as a “national strike” and harbinger of an eventual general strike. Reporting from Ibagué, capital of Tolima Department, he condemns “the criminal ESMAD [riot control police] … [for] violently attacking artists and cultural activists, beating young people, children, and veteran [activists] …They had been chanting slogans against the nefarious government of death and despair. Tear gas flooded the park, spreading panic and state-sponsored terror.” Elsewhere, the police assaulted reporters and human rights defenders, arrested demonstrators, and employed tear gas, stun guns, and rubber bullets. In Medellín,tanks were used. A BBC report catalogues specific actions and interests of Colombia’s new government that are likely to be provoking opposition. A listing follows: • The government is preparing for cuts to the minimum wage and pensions. Concrete proposals are still lacking. • The government will no longer implement its 2016 Peace Agreement with former FARC leftist insurgents. Nor will it cooperate with the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, part of that agreement. • It prioritizes military action against armed groups and henceforth will not negotiate with the remaining leftist insurgencies and dissident FARC groups. • The government broke diplomatic relations with Nicaragua and Cuba and restored relations with Israel, whose influence in Colombia grows. • Colombia’s government is entering “a ‘cultural battle’ … [in favor of] traditional family values and Christian morality” • The new government joined the US-initiated Shield of the Americas, vehicle for US military intervention in the entire region • The report states that De la Espriella “does not dismiss [the idea] of Colombia withdrawing … from in the United Nations, the Organization of American States, and the Interamerican Court of Human Rights.” A recent flurry of “extrajudicial executions ” accompanying police and military actions outraged many Colombians. The BBC offers few details about Colombia’s tightened relationship with the U.S. government. Colombia’s new government has re-committed to joint US-Colombian war on drug traffickers. The US government, however, has long regarded its “drug war” as pretext for engaging leftist insurgents militarily and for providing support generally to Colombia’s military. As reported by the New York Times on October 14, 600 US troops will be heading soon to Colombia where they will carry out training exercises with the Colombian military. De la Espriella’s government has resurrected the failed approach of fumigating coca fields with carcinogenic glyphosate. His government’s military alignment with the US signals complicity with deadly US attacks on small coastal vessels supposedly carrying drugs. Colombia’s new government will likely grant free rein to US corporations, including extractive industries. The plundering that results would aggravate damage already visited upon Colombian land and the environment. Nelson Lombana Silva sounds the alarm: “In a short time, the illegal and mafia-like government of Abelardo de la Espriella has done so much harm … [I]n addition to surrendering national sovereignty, it has been giving away natural resources left and right, exposing the nation’s land to the risk of being turned into a vast desert … Oil and precious metals have fallen into the hands of imperialism thanks to the treacherous, sell-out policies of that clown of a president, Abelardo de la Espriella. He speaks Spanish but thinks in English.” This last remark is shorthand for identifying the president as a US citizen, longtime Miami resident, and wealthy lawyer. He made big money defending extradited Colombian narcotraffickers and top-level paramilitary chieftains in US courts. Lombana Silva resumes: “Counter-reform marches on with increased fracking, lay-offs of 700,000 workers, the highlands and water reservoirs being devastated, ecosystems destroyed, public education privatized, and dumbing down of students with religious indoctrination so they will no longer be thinking, critical individuals, but will remain submissive to Uncle Sam’s dictates .” Looking at the larger context, Professor Restrepo suggests that demonstrations in Colombia and Europe “represent the historical antagonism between capital … as led by government officials subordinate to the club of multi-billionaires allied with colonialist states, on one side, and on the other, the common people who … suffer exploitation, inequality, injustice, discrimination, exclusion, alienation and repression.” He adds that, “Out of that resistance arose the right to rebellion (to take up arms … and the right to social, civil, and unarmed protest.” Restrepo finds affirmation in, of all places, the United States, specifically in Henry David Thoreau’s Civil Disobedience (1849). He quotes: “All men recognize the right of revolution; that is, the right to refuse allegiance to, and to resist, the government, when its tyranny or its inefficiency are great and unendurable.” -W.T. Whitney Jr. is a retired pediatrician and political journalist living in Maine. The post Demonstrations throughout Colombia Target New President and US Intervention appeared first on MLToday .

articles.title: The French People Are Taking to the Streets — But Where is a Communist Party to Lead Them?
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Nikos Mottas October 24, 2026 In Defense of Communism France is once again a country of protests, strikes and growing popular anger. Young people are mobilizing against deteriorating schools and an increasingly uncertain future, while workers confront austerity, rising living costs and attacks on public services. The French state finds enormous resources for military expenditure, yet workers and their families are told that sacrifices are unavoidable. There is no shortage of people willing to fight. What is missing, however, is a powerful revolutionary Communist Party, rooted in the working class and guided by Marxism-Leninism, capable of giving these struggles a clear socialist direction. This absence is particularly striking in France. The country of the Paris Commune, the great workers’ strikes and May 1968 possesses one of Europe’s richest revolutionary traditions. For decades, the French Communist Party (PCF) was a formidable political force, with deep roots in factories, trade unions and working-class neighborhoods. How did a party with such a history end up abandoning the revolutionary principles that once distinguished it from social democracy? The answer lies in a long process of ideological retreat. In 1976, the PCF formally abandoned the dictatorship of the proletariat, a fundamental concept of Marxist theory concerning the conquest and exercise of political power by the working class. Its adoption of the opportunist trend of Eurocommunism, its gradual distancing from the October Socialist Revolution and its increasing reliance on parliamentary alliances marked a decisive turn toward reformism. The revolutionary overthrow of capitalist power was progressively replaced by the pursuit of governmental participation and reforms within the existing system. This was not simply a matter of theoretical declarations. The PCF joined Socialist-led governments under François Mitterrand and later Lionel Jospin. In 1999, while NATO bombed Yugoslavia, the party condemned the aggression but remained in the French government that supported the military operation. Few episodes better illustrate the contradictions of trying to oppose imperialist policy while participating in the administration of an imperialist state. The same political orientation has persisted through successive electoral arrangements with the Socialist Party and, more recently, Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s political forces. The New Popular Front of 2024 was another expression of a strategy that increasingly treats parliamentary combinations and the prospect of a more progressive government as the answer to France’s social and political crisis. But replacing one bourgeois government with another does not change the class that holds power. Nor does a reformist program, however radical its language, constitute a revolutionary alternative to capitalism. The fundamental issue is not whether communists should fight for reforms or cooperate tactically with other forces. It is whether such struggles serve an independent strategy for workers’ power or become ends in themselves. Here lies the significance of the present mobilizations. Students protesting teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and deteriorating educational facilities are confronting the consequences of political choices made in the interests of capital. Workers resisting austerity and declining living standards confront the same system. Yet indignation against particular government policies, even when expressed through mass demonstrations and strikes, does not automatically develop into socialist consciousness. Lenin understood this distinction. In What Is To Be Done? (1902), he insisted that “Without revolutionary theory there can be no revolutionary movement.” The task of a revolutionary party is not merely to support workers’ immediate demands, but to connect their daily struggles with the necessity of overthrowing capitalist class power. Without such political leadership, even powerful movements can be exhausted, diverted into parliamentary expectations or confined to temporary concessions. This is why the historical evolution of the PCF matters today. The consequences of revisionism cannot be measured only in lost votes or parliamentary seats. They are also visible in the weakening of an independent revolutionary perspective within the French working-class movement. A party may retain its communist name, symbols and historical references while pursuing a strategy that no longer challenges the foundations of bourgeois rule. Of course, France is not without sincere communists, militant organizations or workers committed to revolutionary politics. The communist flags visible in the demonstrations themselves testify to the continued presence of revolutionary traditions and political potential. Yet flags alone cannot provide political direction. Without a strong Marxist-Leninist vanguard party, that potential remains fragmented and unable to develop into an organized revolutionary force. And this is the central contradiction. France has fighting workers, rebellious youth and a society marked by sharpening class antagonisms. It also has a Communist Party whose long retreat into reformism has left a profound political vacuum. What is urgently needed is not another electoral coalition promising to administer capitalism more humanely, but the strengthening and rebuilding of a revolutionary communist force, independent of bourgeois politics, with deep roots among workers and youth. The French people are demonstrating that they have not forgotten how to fight. But courage, militancy and mass participation, indispensable as they are, cannot substitute for revolutionary organization and leadership. The task facing French communists is to overcome decades of revisionist retreat and build a genuine Marxist-Leninist vanguard capable of turning resistance into a conscious struggle for workers’ power. France does not lack the forces of struggle. It lacks the revolutionary Communist Party capable of leading them toward the overthrow of the exploitative capitalist system, with the prospect of socialism-communism. -Nikos Mottas is the Editor-in-Chief of In Defense of Communism . articles.title: Why US soldiers keep killing women in Okinawa — and why they go unpunished
articles.author: Amanda Yee
articles.content: In October, 39-year-old Ann Yagi was found dead in a Naha hotel. Shortly after, US marine Devin Jacob Ballard was arrested on charges of murder-robbery. But the Yagi’s killing reignited a decades-old question Okinawa can’t escape: Who pays the price for Washington’s military bases? Okinawan scholar and peace activist Keiko Yonaha joins Amanda Yee to lay out what the headlines leave out — countless sexual assaults by US soldiers and near-total impunity, a Japanese government that covers up case after case, and what Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s rapid militarization means for an island already marked as a potential battlefield. Yonaha also takes direct aim at the new Cold War narrative driving it all, arguing there is no “China threat” to Okinawa or Japan, that the story is being amplified by right-wing trolls and pro-government media to manufacture consent for war. The real danger, she warns, is the US strategy seeking to turn Japan and Okinawa into a frontline for war with China.
